#8744. Skip the Gimmicky Bike Gifts. Our Editors Recommend These 20 Useful Picks Under $50

Useful, cyclist-approved picks that feel thoughtful without blowing your holiday budget.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

As a lifelong cyclist, I’ve received well-intentioned bicycle-themed presents that sit around unused, get forgotten in my closet, or are regifted or donated years later. If you’re shopping for a Christmas or birthday gift for a bike rider, buy something they will truly appreciate and actually use.

Admittedly, buying gifts for cyclists isn’t always easy, and every bicycle rider is different. Cycling is often an expensive, gear-heavy activity with many niches and sub-categories, each with particular equipment needs. Resist the temptation to buy a T-shirt with a poorly drawn bike, AI-generated artwork, or a novelty cycling jersey. Instead, choose something they will love. You can find great gifts that show you put in the extra effort, won’t break your budget, or take weeks to arrive.

Here’s a list of 20 of the most helpful, beautiful, fun, and affordable gifts for cyclists under $50; items we’ve tested, loved, and rely on. Want even more great deals on cycling gear and accessories? Bookmark our Best Bike Gear Deals page for sales and discounts from top cycling retailers.

Bells are handy on the bike path, around town, and on the trail. Aussie brand Knog’s Oi bell is discreet, looks good on everything from a commuter to a race bike, and weighs only about 25 grams. Pick up the Oi Classic with a glass-fiber lever or step up to the Oi Luxe with a metal hammer for about $20 more.

Lezyne makes some of our favorite cycling lights for commuting, road, gravel, and mountain biking. However, while super bright and durable, the brand’s lights can be a bit costly. The KTV Drive combo is a lightweight set of front and rear lights to keep riders visible on commutes and in urban environments. They’re rechargeable, have up to 40 hours of runtime, and fit most bikes.

Electric mini inflators have taken the cycling world by storm. These devices let you quickly and precisely air up any bike tire. However, most inflators are a bit too large and heavy to carry in a jersey pocket or seat bag. Although the Pocket SE doesn’t have a pressure gauge, this pint-sized inflator weighs only 90 grams and fills up to four tires per charge.

The Duraglove ETs from Defeet are an awesome addition to any rider’s fall and winter cycling wardrobe. They’re perfect for rides where temperatures are still above freezing but not warm enough to go without gloves. These gloves have rubber grippers (for holding your handlebar in wet conditions) and are touchscreen-compatible with your smartphone or head unit. They’re an excellent value for under $25.

Sometimes the best gifts are high-end versions of normal things you wouldn’t buy for yourself. While only 33 grams and the size of an Allen key, Daysaver’s Essential8 has the same wrenches as your regular multitool. The design uses nested and flippable magnetic bits made from high-quality stainless steel. As a bonus gift, the Essential8 pairs perfectly with the Coworking5 extension.

What started as a homemade, low-sugar, all-natural sports drink is now a player in cycling nutrition. Skratch Labs offers a palatable solution that keeps you hydrated and energized without causing tummy aches. The brand’s formula is designed to replace exactly what you lose through heavy sweating, whether riding outdoors or on the indoor trainer. Skratch offers several flavors (like lemon-lime, orange, pineapple, and more) and seasonal ones (like apple cider).

Want to save weight in your tires or space in your seat bag? TPU tubes are lighter than traditional butyl rubber tubes and roll faster. They also pack down to about half the size of traditional inner tubes, so they’re the perfect spare tube for your flat kit. They’re available in sizes that fit most road, gravel, and mountain bikes.

We were skeptical that $40 shorts could be this good. However, the Black Bibs consistently outperform shorts that cost six times as much. They’re very simple—no fancy fabrics or creative cuts—and that’s why we love them. Made entirely of plain black Lycra with mesh straps and large leg grippers at the cuffs, they don’t look like anything special. However, even after logging over a year in the Black Bibs, one tester consistently reaches for them first.

Toe covers are perfect for days when it’s not quite cold enough for full booties, but you want to keep your toes warm on the ride. Pearl Izumi’s Amfib model is a solid pick; plus, they are reflective for rides after dark. They provide enough stretch to fit over most road shoes (with cleats) and are easy to put on and take off.

The small but mighty Mattone is a great choice for sleek, waterproof, and secure storage. Thanks to its elastic material, you can pack it to the gills or keep a minimal setup and cinch it tight with the Boa dial.

We look for two traits in a good seat bag: Carrying essentials securely without rattling, and mounting under the saddle without moving around. The Speedsleev Ranger 2.0 Small checks those boxes admirably. It has slots for repair items including CO2 and tire plugs, and a larger compartment for spare tubes and multitools. We’ve loaded it with two TPU tubes, a full-size multitool, CO2, and a plug kit, and still have room to spare.

The Wolf Tooth 6-bit hex wrench multitool is a great gift for any maintenance-minded cyclist. With an optional key ring and a sleek profile, the tool is easy to carry on rides (or when asked to fix your nephew’s bike after holiday dinner). It has everything you need for most basic repairs. Plus, it’s made in America, with replacement parts available.

Dynaplug makes the best (and lightest) tubeless tire plugging tools on the market. The Carbon Racer comes pre-loaded with plugs and takes the guesswork out of fixing a tubeless puncture when sealant isn’t working. The Carbon Racer works like the brand's aluminum Racer Pro plug tool but uses lighter (and more cost-effective) nylon and glass-fiber construction.

Stan’s NoTubes is the original tubeless sealant brand and still one of our top overall picks. Most tubeless sealant was designed for mountain bike and gravel tires that run lower pressures. However, road tires typically need more air pressure, which makes punctures and cuts harder to seal. Stan’s latest introduction is optimized for road bikes with 50+ psi and claims to repair holes up to 7.8mm in size.

A foam roller is a must-have accessory for recovery, preventing injury, and staying fresh. “I’ve been using this foam roller for years, and it's still going strong,” said Senior Health & Fitness Editor Jason Griffin. You can use it to work out tension throughout your body, especially on the glutes, quads, and IT band. Griffin also describes a dual purpose for this foam roller: “I even use this as a balance-board base with an old skateboard deck for cross-training days.”

Multitools are incredibly convenient, but can be hard to manipulate in tight spaces or when you need extra torque to loosen a stubborn fastener. This micro ratchet is a smart alternative that can speed up repairs and adjustments. It includes hex sizes: 2-, 2.5-, 3-, 4-, 5-, 6-, and 8mm, plus T10 and T25 Torx bits, a Phillips screwdriver, and two tire levers. Plus, it’s still small enough to stash in a hip pack or hydration pack.

The machined aluminum Sport Mount is a great gift because it has everything we love about K-Edge’s products—it’s functional, looks great, and is priced right. The Sport Mount fits 31.8mm round bars and holds your head unit sleekly out front and aligned with the stem. Unlike cheap mounts, the Sport’s insert is replaceable if damaged.

Socks are always a go-to gift choice when you don’t know what to give someone. Luckily, almost every cyclist needs more riding socks—and Swiftwick makes some of our favorites. The Merino wool Pursuit crew socks keep your feet dry and warm in winter while providing cushioning and compression.

If your giftee doesn’t already have a Buff in their closet to wear as a scarf, headband, or helmet liner, now is a great time to get one—it also works as a face covering when the temperature dips. The stretchy Merino wool fabric is easy to pull up over the mouth and nose as needed, and it wicks moisture to keep you dry.

Do you have a young reader in your life who likes bikes? “The Ragtag Best Friends Bicycle Club” by Marley Blonsky, a cycling advocate and co-founder of All Bodies on Bikes, tells children about Maisel, her sister Zoe, and new friends as she learns that riding her own way makes cycling great.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8743. The 10 Best Trail Running Shoes for Trails, Gravel, and More

Impeccable traction and responsive rides await. These are the shoes we lace up before hitting the trailhead.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

When I lace up for a day on the dirt, I know my trail running shoes are the only thing separating me from the rocks, roots, and miles of pure, unadulterated trail shenanigans. Trail runners, simply put, are just built different. We rack up mud and rocks with our mileage, and that means we expect more from our gear than road runners while simultaneously abusing the hell out of it. Thanks to my location on the East Coast, I get to run on a huge variety of trails, from packed singletrack to rocky technical trails, to muddy backwoods fire roads, to sandy marsh basins. Basically, I hit all the surfaces, so when I’m testing my trail shoes, I’m really digging in, and so is our legion of shoe testers.

This year has been an interesting year for trail running shoes. Thanks to the growing popularity of trail running, there are more coming out than ever before, but because they are so specialized, reviews are generally all over the place. That’s why on this list you will see very specific workouts for every trail running shoe that we recommend. It’s also why I plan on updating it pretty often, and hopefully expanding the list as new shoes come out and we get our wear testers running in them. The major brands we all expect to see on this list are on here: Saucony, Altra, Salomon, and the like, but choosing trail shoes is complicated and personal, so make sure you read through these reviews to determine which are the best trail running shoes for how and where you run.

For over half a century, Runner’s World has been putting shoes through their paces with staff members and our diverse group of wear testers. These are everyday runners who hit the trailhead and make their shoes work. Every shoe I ran in was put through miles of testing based on its specificity—trail, gravel, technical shoes, et cetera. We evaluate for fit, grip, comfort, responsiveness, weather adaptability, and temperature regulation.

The Hoka Speedgoat 7 makes you forget the issues of the 5 and 6. They’ve nailed the fit this time with updated uppers, new midsole foams, and a smarter construction that finally fixes those nagging complaints about the fit and feel. This model is seriously dialed-in now, making it the perfect shoe for flying over dusty, sandy trails where you need reliable grip without the gunk.

Stack height bumps to 36mm heel, 29mm forefoot using supercritical EVA foam for softer landings and snappier energy return, contrasting to the 6’s firmer feel. A winged heel counter and refined jacquard mesh upper with the addition of a gaiter mean these hug securely without hot spots or blisters, ditching the predecessor’s issues.

Vibram Megagrip outsole upgrades to 5mm lugs with deeper siping and wider spacing; they shed sandy dust and rail trail grit effortlessly while biting hardpack and mild roots. No rock plate keeps it light and easy.

Testers hail the 7’s plush stability on dusty rails—lugs channel sand away for consistent traction; new foam eats vibration from chatter without mush. Uppers breathe during hot days and lock miles better than the 6 ever did.

Wear-tester Diane Grim did note they run a bit smaller, so sizing up is recommended for many, especially those hitting long distances, but she loved the improved fit over the 6, and says that “the lug pattern placement was awesome in gripping (trails were snow-covered and snowmobile groomed),” and she “loved how the lugs continue under the toes for pushing off grip.”

“The Speedgoat 7 engulfs your foot, giving you the security and confidence to get the job done,” she says.

The shoe is a great upgrade for singletrack/rail trail runners craving reliability on flowing, gritty paths from our breakdown. It’s less for pure rock slams, but dusty cruisers never felt this good.

Shop Men’s at hoka.com | Shop Women’s at hoka.com

Salomon Pulsar Trail is a win for us for so many reasons, but the entry point of about $140 is hard to beat. It’s built for runners transitioning from roads or tackling milder trails, blending speed with everyday durability.

This shoe rocks a 29mm heel stack and 23mm forefoot (6mm drop), delivering moderate cushion via TPU-based optiFoam². An Energy Blade TPU insert adds responsive pop and stability without bulk, making strides feel snappy yet protected.

The SensiFit upper with Quicklace locks your foot into the shoe—heel to toe—while breathable mesh keeps swamp feet at bay. The All Terrain Contagrip outsole features 4mm lugs for solid grip on dry dirt, gravel, and roots; it sheds mud decently but slips more on wet rocks.

No rock plate keeps weight low at 9.8 ounces, ideal for non-technical runs.

Wear-tester Rebecca Heflin praises the shoe’s comfort, stability, and versatility, wearing it from road to trail.

“The firmness of the sneaker keeps my foot more in place and safe,” she says. “They took a run or two to break in but then were much more flexible. You could ‘feel’ the ground and what you were running on, but still felt comfortable.” This has largely been my experience as well. For a shoe with some heft, it’s nimble and easy to run in.

The Pulsar Trail has a stable ride; it’s plush underfoot and has Salomon’s signature snug fit. Road-to-trail types will love the smooth pavement transitions. It’s perfect for gravel or mixed surfaces from our earlier breakdown.

Shop Men’s on salomon.com | Shop Women’s on Salomon.com

Saucony Peregrine 16 delivers aggressive trail performance with major upgrades, and a less aggressive drop for a closer-to-the-ground feel. It’s our top pick for technical runners hitting rocks, roots, and mud, thanks to the fact that it’s now softer and grippier than ever.

Stack height hits 32mm heel and 28mm forefoot, powered by more Pwrrun foam for smoother cushioning on long hauls. A Pwrrun+ sockliner is made to add another layer of cushioning and, gross enough, smell issues. But I’ve noticed it also helps protect your feet from creepy crawlies and mud incursion. (Creepy crawlies being the most important by a mile.)

The upper has a snug heel and midfoot with a wider forefoot for toe splay, but not too much that it feels unstable or gives you “squishy toes.” They’re using durable, breathable mesh plus enhanced toe and underfoot protection. A Vibram Megagrip outsole with 4mm lugs grips hard on wet rocks, loose dirt, snow, and roots. The traction is significantly improved over prior models despite shallower depth.

A rock guard plate shields from sharp jabs. And contrary to some other plated trail shoes, it doesn’t feel like you’re running on a cement brick. It’s light and protective without compromising foot motion.

Wear-tester Diane Grim says of the Peregrine 16s, “I LOVE this shoe! Right out of the box, amazing! Lightweight, super comfortable, deep responsive vibram lugs.” She added that though the forefoot was stiff, the shoe eventually conformed to her foot after breaking it in. Lastly, she noted the rock plate and cushioning protected her feet from jabs as she ran over sharp rocks.

The Peregrine 16 fits technical trail types perfectly from our breakdown: deep lugs and armor for rocky descents. The shoe is versatile for mixed or singletrack, too.

Shop Men’s at saucony.com | Shop Women’s at saucony.com

I wasn’t sure if I’d like a trail shoe with Adidas’s energy rods. It didn’t feel like a natural pairing, but I’m sold. The impact protection and bit of easy sturdiness they add is genius. The Lightstrike Pro midsole makes the shoe feel fast, peppy, and fun even on unforgiving surfaces.

That’s the thing that keeps surprising me: I can run hard rock trail for hours and my feet just never come up. I train at ultra distances, and that can murder your feet. These just didn’t.

Some of our testers said the fit was narrow. If you’ve got a wide foot, try before you buy. The flip side is the upper mesh wraps really well once it breaks in, so you get that molded, locked-in feel without cranking the laces. Breathability is fine. Not stuffy, not airy either. On a hot day you’ll notice it.

Where I’d hesitate is technical scrambling: Anything steep and hands-on, anything where you’re placing a foot on an edge and trusting it, and the height and softness start working against you—it gets tippy.So: long runnable rocky stuff, absolutely. Chunky scrambles, I’d grab something lower and firmer.

Altra Experience Wild 3 is a fave for road-to-trail trekkers, making mixed surfaces like macadam, packed gravel, and light dirt paths seem easy. Its low-drop design and wide toebox allow for natural strides on urban-trail mashups without the clunk of pure trail beasts.

Stack height clocks 32mm with cushioned but snappy Ego P35 foam for responsive cushion that feels efficient, not mushy. An extremely subtle rocker aids smooth transitions from asphalt to gravel chatter.

The engineered mesh upper fits securely yet roomy up front, with durable overlays and gaiter traps to block debris on chip seal or cracked pavement trails. MaxTrac outsole packs 4mm lugs that grip macadam’s rough texture, dry gravel, and hardpack without slipping, shedding light mud pretty decently. No rock plate keeps it nimble, prioritizing speed over heavy armor.

Wear-tester John Mikovits raves about the Experience Wild 3, saying, “I loved the way the shoe slipped onto my foot and laced up. The upper felt plenty roomy like many within the brand but also felt secure in the midfoot and heel.

“The midfoot felt secure which kept me in place when pivoting, turning, and both up/downhills,” he added. “I felt secure for the whole ride and really did not notice any feeling of lack of stability or [the shoe being] too loose.”

Daily training, tempo efforts, or 10 to 20 mile mixed runs thrive here; it’s forgiving for road runners dipping into trails. Though less ideal for steep tech or deep slop, it crushes with efficiency and comfort on crumbly-heavy routes that blend pavement and dirt.

Lululemon Wildfeel is a truly versatile trail shoe that’s made for runners who live on flowing singletrack and smooth rail trails. It combines plush comfort and reliable grip for those easy, sometimes muddy, sometimes sandy miles where the path can be unpredictable, and staying nimble is key.

The midsole has dual-density supercritical foam with a cushier heel for shock absorption, and a firmer forefoot for responsive toe-off. This setup helps with stability on undulating singletrack and groomed rail trails.

The sock-like Nulu-lined upper with Lycra-nylon hugs your ankle, acting sort of as a gaiter to block debris on dusty, buggy singletrack. The high-abrasion outsole has 4mm multi-directional lugs that bite reliably on dry dirt, roots, and hardpack rail paths, handling light mud and uneven sections without making you feel wibbly-wobbly.

Tester Ryan Werling loves the Wildfeel, saying, “I looked forward to my runs in this shoe and I felt very confident on any surface (declines/inclines). I have tested some very good trail shoes in this program but the Wildfeel is number one so far.” He did note a less-breathable upper, but here’s the thing: that sealed upper makes it perfect for handling super gross surfaces and sandy marsh trails.

The Wildfeel is less suited for super-technical steeps or deep slop. However, it nails versatile, fun performance on singletrack/rail trail.

Shop Men’s at lululemon.com | Shop Women’s at lululemon.com

Nike’s ACG (All Conditions Gear) line has leveled up lately, and the Zegama Trail is where I’m the most impressed. When the ground turns to oatmeal and the grass is banana-peel slippery, this is the shoe I reach for. The Vibram outsole and aggressive, opposed checkmark lugs dig into packed dirt, wet rock, and sloppy singletrack without ever clogging up. They stay clean and grippy so you can point your nose downhill and trust it.

The revised last is the real upgrade over the old model: it cups the outer rim of your foot so completely that it almost reads as a stability shoe underfoot. A stitched finger loop at the heel makes them easy to yank on, and they breathe well without feeling drafty. My one nitpick is a split in the lug pattern near the heel you can feel on steep descents. They’re a touch heavier than past versions, but I never noticed once moving. As tester Chris Fisher put it, “a solid comfortable trail shoe that I have enjoyed.”

The Mount To Coast H1 absolutely shreds as a gravel specialist, engineered for lightning-fast fire roads and packed paths where loose stones and chatter try to throw you off your game. Its 6mm drop and minimalist build turn rugged gravel into a smooth, efficient run zone that’s ditching the bulk of tech-trail shoes.

Stack height measures 28mm heel, 22mm forefoot, and has a firm, responsive CircleCell foam midsole that delivers sharp ground feel and peppy energy return on washboard gravel. And a wide toebox is a big bonus for folks who love brands like Altra and Topo.

The shoe weighs a scant 7.5 ounces for endless miles.

Testers love its razor-sharp handling on gravel—lugs lock in loose stones for zero slip, moderate drop eases calf strain on long efforts, low stack eats vibrations from rutted fire roads, and wide base shrugs off camber without wobble.

“The fit and comfort of the Mount To Coast is superb,” says tester Liz Fones. “The length felt true-to-size, and the width was generally well-balanced, offering plenty of room without feeling sloppy.”

The H1 is a quintessential gravel shoe: light, grippy, and built for speed on packed dirt and crunchy paths.

Missiongrip outsole deploys 2.5mm lugs with cleat-like clusters that grip wet slabs, mud, and talus, while self-cleaning aggressively. The shoe is tank-like yet responsive.

It’s built for comfort and brutality, and I plan on maxing both out.

The Norda 055 is what happens when someone asks, “What if a hyper-technical trail shoe had a really good stack?” It’s an actual max-cushion mountain shoe with a 36mm stack in the heel and 30mm stack in the forefoot, so your quads get a soft landing while the rest of you commits to the descent.

The preferred shoe of ultrarunner Rachel Entrekin, the upper is woven from bio-circular Dyneema, a fiber with a strength-to-weight ratio 15 times that of steel. You can’t kill these shoes, and I know this because I’ve done my best to try. Trail shoes consist of four main parts: uppers, midsoles, outsoles, and rock plates. These components work together for protection, cushioning, traction, and durability on everything from gravel to gnarly singletrack.

Uppers form the breathable shell around your foot. They feature tough mesh with rubber overlays at the toes and heels to fend off rocks, roots, and trail debris while staying ventilated.

Midsoles provide the cushioning core, typically using EVA foam or advanced compounds like TPU or supercritical foams. They absorb shock from uneven ground and return energy to keep your legs fresh over long miles.

Outsoles are the grippy foundation with lugs made from sticky rubber compounds such as Vibram Megagrip. Lug depth and pattern vary by terrain: multidirectional for mud, clustered for rocks, all designed to shed debris and last through abrasion.

Rock plates sit between midsole and outsole as thin shields of plastic, aluminum, or carbon fiber. They protect against sharp stones and roots without adding much weight or stifling flexibility. With max cushioned trail shoes, they’re not necessarily a must-have anymore, though many runners still prefer them. They don’t exist in every trail shoe, and in the case where a trail shoe may have a carbon plate, it can add protection and stability.

Trail shoes specialize by terrain to optimize weight, grip, and protection. Choosing the right type means less slip, less fatigue, and more fun no matter the surface.

Drop refers to the heel-to-toe height difference, ranging from 0mm (zero drop for natural foot positioning) to 15mm (higher for calf relief on roads or long efforts). Low drops (0 to 4mm) build foot strength but demand adaptation; 8 to 12mm suits most runners.

Stack height measures total midsole thickness underfoot, outsole, and footbed—usually 20 to 35mm at the heel and slightly less at the forefoot. Max stack (30mm+) offers plush protection for heavy runners or rocky miles; low stack (under 25mm) delivers precise ground feel for agile, technical runs.

Gore-Tex and similar membranes laminate into uppers to block liquid water and wind while venting sweat vapor for a little bit of breathability. They shine in rain, snow, or mud, often paired with mesh drainage ports and quick-lace systems to handle stream crossings without sogginess.

I’ve scrubbed enough mud from lugs to write a whole damn article on it, because nothing tanks your trail high like dried clumps firing off mid-stride. Hit them with the hose right after runs to loosen crud and clean them off. Use an old natural bristle brush and mild soap to excavate lug crevices, then stuff with newspaper or paper towels to speed drying. Never toss in the washer; it wrecks glue and mesh. Insider hack: let the muddiest shoes that you can’t get to right away dry out and then bang off the mud. It works, I promise.

#8740. Herniated Discs Are a Common Cycling Injury—Here’s Everything You Need to Know

Keep your back health on track with these tips from top docs and bike-fit experts.

Sometimes it happens with a bang, like when former Tour de France pro Marty Jemison was racing Tour of Flanders in the late 1990s. His saddle slipped to be nose up. He thought “no big deal” until one of the steep cobbled climbs, where he was in the saddle cranking out maximum wattage.“And my back just popped,” he says.

Jemison finished the race and the others that followed until he retired about 18 months later, though he had pain off the bike and for the first 30 or 60 minutes of riding, and knew something was wrong. That something was a herniated disc that became nearly debilitating after retirement, eventually required two procedures, and still flares up to this day if he’s not meticulous about his bike position and on top of his core work.

Other times, it’s the proverbial straw that breaks the camel’s (or the cyclist’s) back, as was the case with avid long-distance cyclist Mark Elsasser of Philadelphia who developed some sciatica in 2018. He was able to ride through it just fine, but couldn’t sit for any length of time before the pain was unbearable. The diagnosis: a herniated disc in his low back, which he resolved with physical therapy and has kept at bay by changing his position on the bike, going from a 0-rise to 5-degree stem. “My spine is less compromised being a bit more upright rather than nose down on top of the stem,” he says.

Herniated discs are fairly common in the general population, occurring most frequently among 30- to 50-year-old adults, and men more often than women. Interestingly, you may have one right now and not even know it. “We know from radiographical studies that 50 percent of those aged 40 may have some form of disc herniation. We might consider it normal, age-related changes, and many of those won’t be symptomatic,” says bike fitter and sports physiotherapist Bianca Broadbent, co-owner of The Cycling Physios based in the United Kingdom.

In fact, one research review published in the American Journal of Neuroradiology found that degenerative changes in the discs, which include herniated discs, are present in nearly 90 percent of adults 60 and older and often require no intervention. A herniated disc only causes pain if it’s pressing or otherwise irritating a nerve root in the spine

Join Bicycling All Access for more injury-prevention tips and training advice!

Your spine is comprised of 24 vertebrae. Between those vertebrae are fluid-filled cushions known as discs, which act as shock absorbers for your spinal bones.

“Imagine your spinal discs as jelly-filled doughnuts,” says Andrew Pruitt, Ed.D., the founder of the Boulder Center for Sports Medicine and CU Sports Medicine and Performance Center. “A herniation happens when the jelly inside pops out.”

You may hear people using other terms like “bulging disc,” “ruptured disc,” or “slipped disc.” Technically, a bulging disc is just that: It’s when the jelly inside the donut is pushing against the side enough to bulge out from the vertebrae but isn’t leaking out. A ruptured or slipped disc refers to an actual herniation, where the doughnut cracks, allowing the gel-filled center to squeeze out.

A bulging and/or herniated disc can cause pain by creating pressure on the nearby nerves. There’s some evidence that the leaked fluid from herniated discs also can cause chemical irritation and inflammation of the spinal nerve roots.

Again, it’s possible to have an asymptomatic herniated disc where you feel no pain. When you do have pain from a herniated disc, however, you’ll know it.

Pain from the herniated discs is sharp and radiating. Most cyclists experience herniated discs in the lower, lumbar back (we’ll get to why in a bit). So you may feel burning pain often known as sciatica that radiates from your lower back into your glutes and down one or both legs, sometimes even into your feet. You may feel pain similar to an electric shock when you stand or sit or walk. You may also feel radiating numbness, tingling, and/or weakness in your lower extremities.

So how does the jelly get out of the doughnut and start wreaking havoc on your spinal nerves? In a word: pressure. It can be extreme and sudden, like Jemison cranking on the cobbles. Or, in many instances, it can happen gradually over time, as was the case with Elsasser.

When your spine is in its generally straight, neutral position, the pressure from the top down is uniform on your discs, so the jelly inside those cushions is evenly distributed, Pruitt explains.

“When you bend forward, the jelly is pushed back, stressing the skin of that doughnut,” he says. “If you’re sitting all day, that jelly is pressing back there for eight hours. Now jump on a bike, and you add another two hours in an even more extreme position, pressing that jelly further and further, until—pop—it comes out.”

Though herniation can happen anywhere in the spine, in cyclists it happens most frequently in the lumbar (low back) region close to the base of the spine, or the L5-S1, the bottom-most disc that sits right on top of your tailbone, because that’s where we bend the most, says Menachem Brodie, C.S.C.S., head coach at Human Vortex Training and USA Cycling expert coach.

“For many cyclists, the L5-S1 is where they’re getting their flexion, and the lumbar spine has about six degrees of movement,” Brodie says. So if you’re not hinging from the hips and keeping your spine within its safe, natural range, you’re pushing those limits. Keeping your spine under that kind of stress for prolonged periods of time pushes you closer to the failure point.

Along those lines, research shows that riders with a lower handlebar position and greater flexion in that key lower back region were more likely to have low back pain. Though, importantly, the research also suggests that poor core strength and endurance could contribute to the spinal stress and low back pain in cyclists.

Of course, the bike isn’t the only place you can stress your spine. The gym can be another place riders put their spine under unhealthy stress, says Dane DeLozier, D.P.T., the biomechanics lab director at and co-founder of Revo Physiotherapy and Sports Performance. Maintaining a stable, neutral spine is very important when resistance training, especially when doing big lifts like deadlifts and squats as well as under velocity like with kettlebell swings, DeLozier says.

“When you have your spine under load, you want it to be neutral and very stabilized. You want to be hinging through your hips, not bending and extending your spine under load,” he says.

If you’re unsure of if you’re maintaining a neutral spine, DeLozier recommends setting up your phone and recording yourself (or having a friend video record you) so you can see if you are breaking or flexing under load.

The good news is a 2020 scientific paper, “Slipped disc: Overview,” reports that about 90 percent of people will get relief from their pain and restricted movement within six weeks even if they receive no medical treatment. That’s because the body gets rid of part of the prolapsed tissue or it shifts position so that the nerves aren’t irritated anymore, according to the overview.

You can help that process along with physical therapy, DeLozier says. “The vast majority of folks feel better and have a great outcome by doing mobility exercises for the hip and low back and decompression exercises for the spine.”

The exercises you do depends on your individual situation, but your physical therapist may recommend mobility, stability, and core strengthening exercises such as:

Press Up: Lie facedown with your feet together, toes pointed, and your forearms on the floor palms. Pull your shoulder blades down and in towards your spine and press into forearms to lift your chest off of the floor, keeping your neck long and hips on the floor. If mobility allows, you can press up further by placing hands below your shoulders to come into an up-dog position. Hold for 3 to 5 seconds. Repeat about 15 times.

Hip Flexor Stretch: Kneel with the affected knee on the floor, tighten your glutes, and brace your abdominal muscles while keeping your back straight. Pressing hips forward. Hold this stretch for 30 seconds. Do 3 times.

Bird Dog: Get on your hands and knees with your palms flat on the floor, shoulder-width apart. Slowly raise and straighten your right leg and left arm at the same time. Keep your hips aligned with the torso and not tilted to one side. Hold for 10 seconds. Return to start. Repeat on the other side.

Cycling itself, when done with a healthy riding posture, can also be a great rehab tool to strengthen the discs and surrounding structures, Broadbent says. In fact, a study done on high-volume road cyclists who rode nearly 100 miles a week for five or more years had beneficial adaptations to their discs and psoas (the biggest hip flexor muscle), which were beneficial for spinal health.

If you’re riding through your rehab, Brodie recommends “crocodile breathing” when you get off the bike. To do it, lie facedown with your forehead resting on the back of your hands and let your chest and hips sink into the floor. Inhale deeply into your belly, expanding your diaphragm for four slow counts. Pause for two seconds, then exhale for six slow counts.

Finally, while many herniated discs can be treated conservatively with physical therapy, some require injection therapy like nerve blocks, if the symptoms are severe, Broadbent says. In rare cases, spinal disc herniation can cause extreme pressure and swelling of the nerves at the end of the spinal cord causing a medical emergency known as cauda equina syndrome.

“If your bladder and bowels aren’t working properly, you have saddle numbness (off the bike as well), or you have sexual dysfunction such as unable to get an erection then you should seek urgent medical investigation,” Broadbent says.

Again, cycling can actually improve spinal strength and the health and hydration of your discs, says Broadbent.

Having a good bike position and the right saddle is key. “You want your spine in a healthy position that doesn’t strain those discs in your lower back,” Pruitt says. If you ride a gravel or a mountain bike, you’re likely already in a slightly more upright, more neutral spine position, he says.

An anatomical saddle will also allow you to put your weight on your perineum without putting harmful pressure on those sensitive tissues, so you’re able to reach the bars without bending too far and putting your spine in an unhealthy position. “Saddle technology improvements have really helped reduce degenerative disc disease,” he says.

You also can protect your spine by doing core-strengthening exercises several times a week. Brodie recommends what are known as the “big three” exercises for spinal stability, developed by renowned back pain expert, Stuart McGill, Ph.D., Professor Emeritus of Spine Biomechanics at the University of Waterloo. These exercises stiffen the musculature throughout the core in a way that enhances stability in the spine.

How to do these exercises: The American Council of Exercise recommends performing three sets for each using a reverse pyramid rep/set scheme. Start with a higher number of repetitions for the first set, then decrease by 2 to 6 reps, then decrease by another 2 to 4 reps on the last set. So you might start with 8-6-4 reps and work your way up to 12-10-8 reps as you get stronger and build endurance. Hold each exercise for no more than 8 to 10 seconds.

McGill Curl-up: Lie on your back with one leg extended and the other leg bent, foot flat on the floor. Put your hands under your low back to maintain your natural arch. In one move, lift your head, shoulders, and chest off the floor, keeping your neck and back in the neutral position. Hold. Then slowly return to start. Do half a set. Then switch legs and complete the set.

Side Bridge: Lie on your right side, with your forearm on the floor and elbow underneath your shoulder. Bend your knees at a 90-degree angle. Place your left hand on the opposite shoulder for stability. Lift your hips off the floor so your body forms a straight line from your head to your knees. Hold. Then lower to the starting position and repeat to the other side. Work up to doing the move with your legs straight.

The Bird Dog: (As explained in the previous section)

You can make these exercises part of your warm-up, along with dynamic mobility moves before you get into your bigger lifts.

Off the bike, Brodie recommends practicing good spine hygiene by avoiding hunching forward when you sit and not sitting in a static position for prolonged periods of time, but rather shifting positions in your chair every 15 minutes and getting up, moving around, and doing a little standing stretch, extending your arms, reaching overhead and taking a deep breath every 60 to 90 minutes.

Finally, don’t overlook your mattress. A firm mattress with a pillow top will help support your spine while you sleep, Brodie says. “A lot of people overlook this and it can make a big difference in your back health.”

#8739. No Medal, No Aid Stations, No Crowd: What a Solo Ironman Through a National Park Taught Me

He swam 2.4 miles, biked 112 miles, and ran a marathon—all by himself, through one of America’s most spectacular national parks.

Late last year, a friend in Seattle suggested we train for an Ironman 70.3 from opposite coasts. He did the runs, swims, and bike rides along the Pacific Ocean, and I followed suit along the Chesapeake Bay. We weren’t sure whether we’d meet in the middle for an organized event in Nebraska, or save on travel costs with an unofficial “Do-It-Yourself” approach in our backyards.

About halfway through training, he dropped out because of a knee injury. I soldiered on. After 16 weeks of prep, I felt ready, so I set out on my own—no aid stations or medals waiting at the finish line—and accomplished the trek to Annapolis, Maryland, and back in the middle of a snowstorm, with 84 laps in the community pool counting as my 1.2-mile swim.

Later on, I moved to Jackson, Wyoming, where my runs, swims, and bike rides would take place in the shadow of the Tetons. I decided to increase my training workload to try for a full-distance Ironman, also DIY, in Grand Teton National Park. I doubled everything from the 70.3 training block except for the weekend long runs. The schedule as written would have quickly had me running marathons the day after punishing bike rides that took half a day and marked my longest-ever distances in the saddle.

It wasn’t easy. Trail runs and lake swims easily eclipsed the distances I’d done for my high school cross country and swim teams, respectively. And the time was hard to schedule around my 9-to-5. I found a few encouraging partners to swim, ride, and bike with, but I did the majority of the sessions on my own.

The joy of training in pristine wilderness, as spring turned to summer, turned out to be solid motivation. After missing only a handful of workouts over 16 weeks, I felt ready.

I had done another solo half-Ironman to get a feel for the course, my gear, and my fitness level. The week before my target DIY attempt on August 8, I raced a short gravel triathlon with some friends in Steamboat Springs, Colorado, placing second in the first-timers category.

The week of my taper, I relaxed with virtually no workouts. On the day of my attempt, unfortunately, a thick smoke from a West Coast wildfire filled the valley. The swim felt fine, and the bike ride was issue-free, but I could feel my lungs working overtime. By the time I started the run, I couldn’t fathom the marathon ahead of me. Temperatures crested at 80°F, and I was dipping my face and hands in every available stream.

Seven miles in, I started walking and, from there, it was all over. Doing an Ironman without any of the pressure of an organized event means it’s much easier to quit at any point. And the moment I FaceTimed my parents to fill them in, I knew I could just as easily come back and try again the following weekend. No pricey entrance fee or travel to make up. This is my backyard.

So I waited for the smoke to clear, made sure to do a more reasonable taper, and tried again the following weekend, with some of the nerves already shaken out.

Sure, these are luxuries I wouldn’t have had if I’d done a “real” Ironman. But it’s certainly in line with the ethos of these mountains: Sometimes it’s not your summit day. Buoyed by a friend’s words of encouragement (“You have the fitness; you just need a better day”), I packed up the car again and set off for Jenny Lake.

This time, I had my nutrition more dialed: instead of 20-gram protein bars, I packed apple slices and an egg sandwich. The smoke was gone and overcast skies kept temperatures cool. Halfway through the bike ride, a light rain helped chill me even more.

One hundred miles in, disaster struck. My bike’s rear wheel went flat. Rookie road cyclist that I am, I had failed to heed the advice of a more experienced friend to invest in a patch kit. But the trail gods were smiling on me. I pulled right into the Jackson Lake Lodge, where, to my great luck, a pair of bikepackers on their way down the Continental Divide were happy to share some basic supplies.

In 30 minutes, I was back on the way to Jenny Lake, and made it into the parking lot—just as the tire went flat again. I nervously glanced at the odometer: 112.05 miles. Phew!

I felt I owed it to my trail fairy Don to complete the challenge at this point. In a break from official Ironman rules, I allowed myself headphones and music, figuring they were replacing some of the hype of fellow competitors and spectators on a real course.

After 26.2 medium-speed miles, I clicked stop on my watch and collapsed into the cool waters of Jenny Lake as the pink hues of sunset framed the mountains that had been my guide.

“I will forever be a changed man,” I thought to myself. I slept in late the next day, and returned to work on Monday, proud but mostly unchanged. What followed might surprise you.

As the days became shorter and the water colder, a next goal failed to materialize. I fell off my tri-sport routine and started to tick off a few longer hikes instead. I don’t know if I’ll ever do an actual, sanctioned Ironman.

I admire the YouTubers who inspired me to keep up with my training. I understand the appeal of qualifying for the championships in Hawaii. For me, I was simply curious if my body could string together the distances. It was enough that my friend in Seattle called me a beast.

Oddly, I didn’t feel stronger, or more disciplined, or more motivated than when I had started. It was great to have a distraction from work and the chance to push myself in another realm. But, absent others doing the exact same things at the same time, the distances felt arbitrary.

One blessing of living so close to a national park is there are countless adventures and challenges nearby. A few years ago, I tried my hand at the Teton Triathlon. Also known as The Picnic, this unsanctioned endeavor starts with a 20-mile bike ride to Jenny Lake, which you swim across before climbing Grand Teton, the tallest mountain in the range (its summit is 13,775 feet, about 7,000 feet above the Jackson valley), before descending and doing it all in reverse, swimming back across the lake (about 1.2 miles) and biking back to town. It took me 22 hours, and I’d do it again in a heartbeat.

There’s nowhere else in the country you can do anything quite like it. And, to me, the point is to test yourself, rather than beat a field of neoprene-clad athletes. The joy of completing even an unsanctioned Ironman in Grand Teton National Park paled in comparison to the deep satisfaction I felt after completing The Picnic.

A few friends told me it was more impressive to do the Ironman without competitors and fans urging me on. I understand how the public nature of competition helps some people push through hard training days and the race itself. I don’t know that it would have made a difference for me.

When I ran the Chicago Marathon a few years ago, the mandatory fundraising gave that race meaning. I wasn’t bummed that I didn’t qualify for Boston because I’d still hit my dollar goal.

A few weeks after this summer’s Ironman, I accompanied a man running a 50K route in every state in 50 days to raise $1 million for charity. He said that, after a few years of ultramarathons, he wanted to give his time and effort a greater purpose, and doing it for the Make-A-Wish Foundation did that.

That single slow, conversational 50K holds as much meaning for me as all the work I did for my own Ironman. Maybe because it’s a fraction less selfish. Or maybe because it was shared.

That experience, and that man, have stayed with me. I think both of us are chasing something similar in our non-running lives.

#8737. Can the Tour Be Pogačar-Proofed? The 2027 Tour de France Route Is Designed to Keep the Racing Close.

More time trialing and fewer summit finishes could give Remco Evenepoel, Jonas Vingegaard, and the rest of the peloton a chance to take the fight to the five-time champion.

It’s early November, which means the Halloween candy is on sale, the piles of leaves in my yard are getting harder to ignore, and the routes for the 2027 men’s and women’s Tour de France have finally been unveiled. After weeks of refreshing Tour rumor sites, here’s what stood out to me about the men’s route.

First, let’s address the Slovenian elephant in the room: There’s little anyone can do to defeat a healthy, in-form Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates XRG), who will head into the 2027 Tour as the overwhelming favorite to take a record-breaking sixth overall victory. Certainly, the organizers seem to feel the same way.

Rather than create a race designed to defeat him, which currently doesn’t seem possible, they’ve laid out a course that could at least prevent the five-time champion from running away with it in the first week. The 2027 Tour packs more than 53,000 meters of elevation gain and 28 second-, first-, or hors catégorie climbs into its 21 stages. But there are only three summit finishes, and the first doesn’t arrive until the end of Stage 9, atop the Grand Colombier.

That means fewer chances for Pogačar and his team to jump out to a huge early lead on the Tour’s general classification and then ride defensively, slowly wearing down the opposition until the final week. That’s when the Slovenian usually delivers the coup de grâce, adding a few more stage wins to his ever-growing tally.

Yes, there are a couple of punchy uphill finishes in the opening week, at the end of Stages 4 and 5, and Pogačar will do well on them. But the time gaps shouldn’t be huge, so I expect a tighter bunch of riders at the top of the GC heading into the first individual time trial on Stage 7.

Speaking of time trials, the 2027 Tour features 71 kilometers of them across Stages 7 and 16, the most we’ve seen since 2012. It’s hard not to see that as a nod to Belgium’s Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull–Bora–Hansgrohe), the four-time world time trial champion who finished second in the Tour this past July.

If he can improve his preparation for this year’s Tour, and he’s only 26, Evenepoel could use those time trials to his advantage. The first might even give him a chance to give Pogačar a scare before the mountains arrive at the end of the opening week.

But waiting until Stage 9 for the first mountain stage doesn’t mean the opening week will be easy. A slew of long, tricky stages will be tough for one or two teams to control. And at least until the Stage 7 time trial, plenty of riders should be in contention to spend a day or two in yellow and willing to take a few risks and big swings to make it happen. That’s the downside of designing a route that attempts to delay the GC fireworks until the second week. More riders feel they have a chance to wear yellow, which can lead to more risk-taking and, unfortunately, the possibility of more crashes.

Throw in tight roads, punchy climbs and descents, some rain during the three opening stages in the United Kingdom, and perhaps a few days of crosswinds, and you’ve got the exact right mix to create unpredictable and downright chaotic racing.

If Pogačar is going to run away with another Tour, I expect we’ll know by the end of Stage 11, the final day in the Alps and the second of the race’s three summit finishes. If his rivals, including Evenepoel, Denmark’s Jonas Vingegaard (Visma–Lease a Bike), and France’s Paul Seixas (Decathlon CMA CGM Team), can somehow limit the damage on Stages 9, 10, and 11, we could have a much more compelling Tour than what we’re used to.

A run of sprint and transitional stages follows before the final week, when the second time trial and two days in the Pyrenees await. With any luck, we’ll still have a GC battle worth watching by then.

That’s what the organizers appear to be hoping for with this route. But given what we’ve seen from Pogačar and his UAE squad in recent Tours, I’m not sure it will happen. While the time trial kilometers seem to acknowledge Evenepoel as one of Pogačar’s greatest threats, I also see the route as a not-so-subtle gesture to Seixas, the young Frenchman many consider the rider most likely to be Pogačar's successor.

Seixas, now 20, raced his first Tour this past summer and finished fourth overall. The 2027 course should give him a chance to continue growing as a Tour contender without throwing him in at the deep end the way this year’s route did. The French would be thrilled to see him finish on the final podium, and with the Tour’s most intense stages broken into two- or three-day chunks, with time to recover and regroup in between, that kind of result looks well within his reach.

I’m also eager to see how two-time Tour champion Vingegaard tackles the race. Recent routes have forced Vingegaard and his Visma–Lease a Bike team to burn a lot of matches early, leaving them powerless when Pogačar and his UAE teammates throw down in the second and third weeks. The 2027 course should allow Vingegaard to ride a bit more under the radar, hopefully keeping him fresh for the Stage 7 time trial and the first summit finish on Stage 9. If all goes to plan, the Dane could enter the third week ready to challenge Pogačar in a way we haven’t seen since Vingegaard won his second Tour in 2023.

As for specific stages, I’ve already marked a few as days I won’t want to miss.

The Tour begins in the United Kingdom with three stages that should generate some intense battles among sprinters and Classics riders. Of the three, Stage 3 looks like the hardest. Its 223 km route includes a slew of punchy climbs, making it a perfect day for riders like Mathieu van der Poel (Alpecin–Premier Tech), Wout van Aert (Visma–Lease a Bike), and Tom Pidcock (Pinarello–Q36.5 Pro Cycling Team).

Then there’s Stage 10, a 171 km ride from Annecy to Sallanches that features six categorized climbs and previews the course used in August’s world championship road race. Coming right after the Tour’s second rest day and sandwiched between summit finishes on Stages 9 and 11, this should be an exciting and hard-to-predict day for the GC contenders.

Stage 14 takes the riders 199 km from Montpellier into the Cévennes, covering many of the roads immortalized in Tim Krabbé’s The Rider, one of the best cycling novels ever written. Seriously, if you’ve never read it, find a copy and enjoy! The stage ends on an airstrip just past the summit of the Côte de la Croix Neuve, a famous climb that always generates an exciting finish.

After taking a back seat in recent Tours, the Pyrenees close out the mountain racing in 2027, highlighted by Stage 18. The Tour’s “queen stage” runs 174 km from Pau to Saint-Lary-Soulan, with 5,400 meters of elevation gain and perhaps the two toughest climbs in the entire race: the Col du Tourmalet and a summit finish on the Col du Portet. If the race hasn’t been decided heading into Stage 18, it should be by the end, even with one relatively milder day in the Pyrenees still to come.

And what about Stage 21? Maybe you heard the pre-announcement rumors that the organizers would skip the cobbled Côte de la Butte Montmartre. Thank goodness they proved false. Adding a few trips over the climb to the final stage in 2025 has proven to be one of the greatest innovations in Tour history, and I’m thrilled they kept it in for another year.

Overall, the 2027 men’s Tour stacks up like this: 3,479 kilometers (2,162 miles) spread over 21 stages, with seven flat stages, six hilly stages, six mountain stages, two individual time trials, and three rest days.

With about eight months to go before the riders hit the road in Edinburgh, a lot can still happen. Most of the top contenders haven’t even confirmed their 2027 programs, which means there’s a chance, however unlikely, that at least one of them might not participate.

But as long as Pogačar is racing, the result, for better or worse, might be a foregone conclusion. And that’s not necessarily a bad thing. He is a once-in-a-lifetime talent, resetting the record books of the sport the way Eddy Merckx once did.

But as the saying goes: it’s the journey—not the destination—that matters here. Yes, we should enjoy speculating about who will and who won’t win the Tour de France—and how and when they manage to do it. But we can’t forget that the Tour de France offers at least 21 chances for something exciting and unexpected to unfold. Next year’s route might not prevent the inevitable, but it will certainly produce lots of great racing along the way. And I can’t wait.

#8736. Training on Fatigued Legs Builds Durability—as Long as You Do It Right. Experts Explain How.

These expert-backed strategies help you use fatigue to build speed endurance without risking injury.

Most runners know the feeling: dragging yourself out for a jog when your legs feel like lead.

Your calendar says it’s supposed to be an easy day, but your quads seem to have missed the memo. You settle into a shuffle, wondering how a pace that felt effortless last week could demand so much today.

“Running on tired legs means that your body is in a state of recovery following an effort or stimulus,” says Brad Whitley, DPT, a doctor of physical therapy and clinic director at Bespoke Treatments in San Diego. That effort might come from a hard run or strength session, but emotional and work stress can also contribute, he says.

A run in that state isn’t necessarily a bad idea. Practicing on tired legs can help prepare you for the later miles of a race, when you no longer feel fresh. The trick is knowing when pushing through fatigue is useful to performance—and when a rest day will do you more good.

Simply put, running through some fatigue makes you stronger, both physically and psychologically.

“Running on tired legs helps build resilience in the muscular system,” explains Victoria Sekely, DPT, CSCS, a doctor of physical therapy and certified run coach based in New York City. A more resilient muscular system means your muscles can not only recover faster, but also carry you longer and at a quicker clip.

“When your legs are tired, your muscles are undergoing a biophysiological change,” Sekely explains, which includes building stronger muscle fibers. “If you keep going past that fatigue, that will end in a positive adaptation—meaning you can start to run longer without the fatigue setting in.”

Whitley agrees and highlights the mental benefits: “One of the benefits of running on tired legs can be psychological—that is, teaching your central and peripheral nervous systems [the brain, spinal cord, and all nerves that extend to the rest of the body] that you are able to operate with higher levels of fatigue,” says Whitley. “This is helpful for longer races like a half marathon, marathon, ultramarathon, Ironman, and more.”

While it has its benefits, this training tactic requires thoughtful execution to avoid overtraining or injury.

Whatever you do, if you’re running on tired legs, keep the effort easy. “As a rule of thumb, runners shouldn’t complete high-intensity sprints or long threshold sessions when fatigued, as these types of workouts are when muscle strains can happen,” advises Whitley.

Here are a few strategies for how to practice running on tired legs.

“Initially, the best way to introduce training on fatigued legs would be to complete a run in the morning and a whole-body and/or lower-extremity strength session in the afternoon,” says Whitley. “This allows time for some recovery to occur and then would stress a different physiological system in the afternoon.”

It can feel difficult, but your body will become more resilient as the muscle and tendon capacity increases.

The easiest strategy to try running on tired legs is simply to schedule an easy run right after a long training run or speed workout.

“Running on tired legs is mainly for runners who run more than four days a week, and it will naturally happen if you’re following something along the lines of the 80/20 guideline, where 80 percent of your runs are easy and 20 percent are hard,” says Sekely. “On the days that are hard and followed up with an easy day, your legs will most likely feel fatigued. You are certainly at an increased risk of injury on that day, which is why it’s imperative to keep that easy day easy.”

If you’re increasing mileage or prepping for a long-distance race, consider running twice in one day. “Make the morning run a priority, and the p.m. run can be done at an aerobic pace—think zone 1 to 2—to make up for volume needed for the day,” says Whitley.

There’s a fine line between training smart and overtraining. If you’re not fueling properly or skimping on rest, pushing through fatigue is going to backfire, says Sekely.

“It’s important to recognize if you need a rest day—all athletes I work with implement at least one or two rest days every seven to 10 days,” she says. “Every runner benefits from rest days as much as they do easy days.”

Plus, adds Whitley, too much training when you’re feeling tired can mean you’re chronically overtrained—and leave you burned out or with an overuse injury.

So before you head out with heavy legs, check in on a few variables:

Check in with your emotional state before you head out for your run. “If you’re noticing it is incredibly hard to get motivated and you’re having difficulty getting out the door, this might be a sign of chronic fatigue, and you should modify your training schedule,” says Whitley.

Don’t be afraid to take a day or two off, so you feel ready to get back out there.

This is a good guideline to gauge whether you’d benefit more from a run or rest on any given day, says Whitley: If you start your run with moderately fatigued legs and find that you’re not feeling better after moving for 10 minutes, modify the run by making it lower effort (slowing the pace or eliminating hills), or cut it short if you’re seriously struggling.

Heart rate variability measures your individual readiness compared to yourself, and many smartwatches have features to help you easily track yours. If your HRV is way off from your average, Whitley advises opting for a rest day.

When you do call it a day and kick your legs up instead of lacing up to log some miles, remember that you’re not slacking; rest is when the real gains happen.

To get the biggest boost from your time off, Whitley recommends thinking about how you can reduce the root cause of your fatigue—whether that’s doing gentle yoga or getting a massage for sore muscles or meditating to clear a mind that’s been overwhelmed with work stress.

At the end of the day, running on tired legs isn’t about pushing through at all costs—it’s about knowing when to lean into discomfort for growth and when to pull back to avoid burnout.

The core mechanism here is Flying Blue's Promo Rewards program, and once you understand how it works, you'll never look at transatlantic business class the same way again.

Flying Blue is Air France-KLM's frequent flyer program and a member of the SkyTeam alliance. Unlike many loyalty programs that use a static award chart, Flying Blue uses dynamic pricing — meaning award costs fluctuate based on demand, route, and season. That sounds like a disadvantage, and for standard awards it often is. But Flying Blue offsets this with a monthly release of Promo Rewards: a curated list of routes where award seats are released at 25–50% below standard dynamic pricing, often with surcharges waived entirely.

This is the inefficiency. When Air France wants to stimulate demand on a specific route in a given month, it uses Promo Rewards to attract award bookings. The airline gets seats filled; you get business class to Paris for 53,000 miles instead of potentially 80,000+ at standard dynamic rates. It's a win-win — if you know to look for it.

The transfer ecosystem is what makes this accessible. Flying Blue partners with every major transferable points currency at a 1:1 ratio:

The practical implication: if you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Amex Platinum, Amex Gold, Citi Strata Premier, Capital One Venture X, or Bilt Mastercard, you already have a direct pipeline to Flying Blue miles. Most transfers are instant, meaning you can spot a Promo Reward, confirm the seat exists, transfer points, and book — all in the same afternoon. That speed matters because Promo Reward seats can disappear quickly.

One nuance worth naming: fuel surcharges. On standard Flying Blue awards for Air France and KLM-operated flights, the program passes through carrier-imposed surcharges that can add $200–$500 to your redemption. However — and this is critical — Promo Reward bookings typically eliminate these surcharges, meaning you pay the miles cost plus only government taxes. Always confirm surcharge status before booking a non-Promo award.

Finally, understand the routing rules: Flying Blue allows open-jaw itineraries, meaning you can fly into Paris and home from Amsterdam (or vice versa), effectively building a multi-city European trip with a single award booking. The booking window opens 359 days in advance — plan accordingly.

If Promo Reward seats aren't available on your dates, don't give up. Check standard award availability on Flying Blue — the pricing will be higher, but the experience is identical. Alternatively, set up alerts through third-party tools and revisit the search as your travel dates approach. Availability often opens closer to departure as airlines release unsold inventory.

Unlike most airline award programs that set a fixed or dynamic price and leave it, Flying Blue runs a monthly promotional cycle. At the beginning of each month, they release a list of routes with discounted award pricing. These Promo Rewards typically offer 25-40% off the standard mileage price and apply to both economy and business class. The discounted routes change every month, covering different destinations on a rotating basis. This means a route that is not on promotion this month may appear next month. The system rewards patience and monitoring: travelers who check the Promo Rewards page monthly and maintain transfer-ready points in Chase, Amex, or other programs can consistently find premium cabin deals to European destinations.

For popular summer routes, start checking Promo Rewards at month-eight to month-ten before your trip. - **Follow community resources.** The ChooseFI community and frequent flyer forums will alert you when a strong Promo Reward drops — you don't have to monitor alone. - **Practice the search before you need it.** Log into FlyingBlue.com today and run a practice award search. Get comfortable with the interface before you're racing to book a Promo Reward seat. If you can earn miles and check a website once a month, you can execute this redemption. Thousands of travelers in the ChooseFI community have done it — you're next.

Major US-to-Europe routes like JFK-CDG or JFK-AMS tend to appear on the Promo Rewards list every 2-4 months. Less popular routes may appear less frequently. The key is consistent monthly monitoring so you catch the promotion when it appears for your target destination.

Flying Blue does not offer formal stopover benefits on award tickets. However, you can book a one-way promo award to your gateway city and then add a separate low-cost carrier or train connection to your final destination. Many travelers use this strategy to explore Paris or Amsterdam for a few days before continuing onward.

Yes. Flying Blue miles expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Any qualifying activity resets the clock, including earning miles through a flight, credit card transaction, or transfer partner. A single small transfer from Chase or Amex every two years is sufficient to keep your miles alive.

Both airlines offer lie-flat business class seats with direct aisle access on long-haul aircraft. Air France's cabin tends to emphasize French culinary presentation and wine service, while KLM has a more understated Dutch design aesthetic. Both are solid products. When booking through Flying Blue, you can choose either airline based on routing, schedule, or cabin preference.

Flying Blue Promo Rewards turn business class to Europe from a special-occasion splurge into a repeatable system. By monitoring monthly promotions, maintaining transfer-ready points across multiple programs, and booking when your route appears at a discount, you can consistently fly lie-flat to European destinations for 50,000-62,000 miles. The fuel surcharges are a real cost to factor in, but even with that overhead, promo business class awards deliver 5-12 cents per mile in value. Set the monthly reminder and let the system work.

#8734. Your First Gravel Ride Should Feel Like an Adventure—These 3 Tips Will Help You Enjoy It

Gravel takes different prep than road riding—these basics help you ride off road with confidence.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

The more riders I talk to, the more I see people switching over to gravel bikes. I was leading a group ride for a shop in New Jersey and the group primarily consisted of road cyclists on their first gravel ride. The line of the day was, “this is so fun—it’s like being a kid on a bike.” Gravel is challenging, but it’s also a different type of fun once you get off paved roads.

Over the last few years, I’ve focused more on gravel riding than any other discipline of cycling. My lunch rides typically end up being on the road and my strictly fun rides end up being on the mountain bike. But I’ve been gravitating more and more to the gravel bike because it can do a little bit of everything.

I’ve taken gravel bikes on everything from 100-mile road rides with 10,000 feet of climbing to rides on singletrack trails where we should have been on a hardtail mountain bike at a minimum. On bikepacking routes, gravel day rides, and family rides towing my kids in their bike trailer, the gravel bike has been my go-to rig.

If you’re new to the sport, or even just getting into the category of gravel riding, it's easy to feel like there’s a mountain of knowledge needed as a barrier to entry. Here we’ll break down the top gravel tips you need to know to find success in those first few rides and beyond.

When I ran a shop this was the first place I would start with folks who were gravel curious. The touchpoints on a bike are both where you contact the bike and where the bike touches the ground. The pieces of gear to focus on here are: chamois, gloves, saddle, bar tape, and tires.

The chamois and gloves are the first two because they are the parts on your body that touch the bike. I don’t like to use gloves that are overly padded, but I do like gloves that have a good level of tackiness to help with staying gripped to the handlebars. This year I’ve been using the Most Days Full Finger Gloves from Handup for everything from century gravel group rides to hard gravel rides with plenty of singletrack. The chamois can be a little more subjective, but I almost always suggest going with chamois bibs over chamois shorts.

Bibs stay in place better than shorts and this is especially important from the movement you’re doing on a gravel ride. I’ve had plenty of people ask if they really need padded shorts for riding and the short answer is no. You can go riding with regular basketball shorts, but you’ll have a much better time riding with padded shorts or bibs. I like to compare it to riding a road bike on gravel. You can absolutely do that, and for a long time that’s what people did, but there’s a better way. My favorite pair are the Q36.5 Dottore Pro Bibs because they stay in place incredibly well and are comfortable from the first hour in the saddle to the 11th hour. The price point is a realistic hurdle for these Q36.5 bibs, but our Deputy Test Editor at Bicycling, Tara Seplavy, calls out this pair available on Amazon for just $40 in her roundup of cycling shorts.

I personally like a tape that has some tackiness while also offering a bit of cushion for some dampening after miles of chattering gravel. My favorite tape is the Lizard Skin DSP Ultra Bar Tape. It comes in a range of colors and thicknesses, but I usually go with the 2.7mm or 3.5mm for people riding gravel. If you want a little extra comfort over the miles size up to the 3.5mm.

When it comes to saddles this is much more subjective because everyone’s sit bones are different and your preferred saddle can change depending on your position on the bike. Personally I have different saddles on each of my bikes based on how I use that specific bike. The biggest note on saddles is to avoid going with something super wide and overly padded. This can be a desirable thing to reach for after you’ve developed a bit of soreness from your initial rides, but try to avoid the beach cruiser type of saddles. These can cause extra friction and that’s the last thing you want to add to your gravel ride.

Finally, we get to where the bike touches the ground—the tires. When someone is looking to add comfort and versatility to a gravel bike I usually recommend bumping up the tire size. Most bikes don’t come stock with the widest tire you can fit on the bike, so check the technical specifications for your bike to see how wide you can go. Some of my favorite gravel tires are the Pirelli Cinturato H tires and the Continental Dubnital tires for their versatility on a range of terrains.

This is a broad tip, but it is the most all-encompassing piece of advice I can give for gravel. Gravel riding burns more energy mile for mile and climb for climb compared to a road ride. Keep this in mind when you’re putting together your nutrition and hydration plan as well as when you’re building the route. It’s important to bring more calories than you think you need because you’ll likely be burning more calories compared to a road ride; it will take longer to get to the next refill stop compared to what you would expect, and those refuel spots are fewer and farther between on gravel roads and dirt trails compared to a road ride.

When it comes to setting up my route I always suggest riders have a way to navigate. When I got into gravel riding I used my phone for navigation with a handlebar mount on the bars. This worked initially, but because of the mud on some gravel routes, the possibility of falling, and how fast navigating on my phone killed the battery I quickly switched to a dedicated head unit. Head units that are capable of navigating reasonably well can range from a few hundred dollars to just shy of a thousand. Currently I’m testing the COROS Dura 2 Solar and I love the fact that battery life can last for days of solid run time. A dedicated bike computer head unit is something that’s nice to have as you start to adventure, but if you currently have a smartwatch you can likely use that to navigate for now. It’s more convenient having the head unit in front of you for navigation compared to a smart watch. Lately I’ve been trying a few different watches from Garmin and COROS as a substitute for a bike computer and once I set up turn-by-turn notifications I’ve gotten used to navigating by the watch. Plus I can use the watch for other activities like runs, family hikes, and the occasional paddle.

Flat tires will eventually happen on a gravel ride. Step one is to bring a good flat kit with a reliable set of tire levers, a multitool (with a chain breaker), at least one tube, and a pump for inflation. I also typically bring a dollar bill as a backup for a tire boot in the event that I really blow out my tire. Ever since I had to use fallen leaves as a tire boot I always carry something to cover a large hole in the tire.

Step two is knowing how to use the tools you brought. Bringing a chain breaker tool or tire levers are great, but they won’t be much help if you aren’t able to figure out how to use them. When someone was buying a new bike from me I used to encourage them to practice taking the wheels off the bike, tires off the wheels, tubes out of the tires, then putting it all back together. Getting some laps on this process from the comfort of your home will make the process feel much smoother when you’re trying to finish the flat fix on the side of the trail.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. #8732. ’90s vs. Modern Bodybuilding: Why Today’s Pros Wouldn’t Win Pro Cards in the Mass Monster Era

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

On Episode 307 of The Menace Podcast, host Dennis James was joined by Milos Sarcev and Jose Raymond, and the panel compared the current era of competitive bodybuilders with those of the 90s. How would they stack up?

The 90’s was a decade where size dominated the stage. Often referred to as the “Mass Monster” era, stars like Dorian Yates, Lee Haney, and Ronnie Coleman reigned supreme. But how do current muscle men stack up against these icons of the past? Jose Raymond speculated that there may be a drop in quality in the 2020s, because IFBB Pro Cards are too easily won these days. “If you have to fight for a pro card, for seven to ten years, by the time you get it you’ll be ready,” said the bodybuilder-turned-coach. “And the physique is going to be already matured and marinated.”

Raymond felt that younger bodybuilder’s winning pro cards effects the overall talent pool. “The physique isn’t ready,” he said. “Most of today’s guys would not win a pro card in 1993, 1989.”

Agreeing with Raymond’s take, host Dennis James said that “90% of them, maybe even more than 90%,” would not win a pro card if competing in the ’90s. “You’ve got guys getting a pro card for second place,” added Raymond. “That’s crazy to me.”

To further cement this observation, Milos Sarcev explained that respected and revered bodybuilders of the past like Edgar Fletcher and Matt Mendenhall never even turned pro. “Edgar Fletcher would win pro shows today,” said Raymond. “One hundred percent,” agreed Sarcev.

The Menace further explained that there have been more than 70 athletes qualifying for Olympia categories, from a pool of around 500, although this is being tightened up in many divisions with the requirement to win two shows. So, perhaps restoring quality over quantity is the key to creating the best era.

To see this conversation in full on The Menace Podcast, where the panel also discussed the latest bodybuilding news and results, check it out on the Muscle & Fitness YouTube channel.
