#8659. The Glute Training Guide for a Stronger and More Powerful Posterior

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Not every muscle gets immortalized in a rap song, but the glutes do more than look good in pants. Beyond the vanity benefits, the glutes help you do fun things in and out of the gym.

Although the gluteus maximus gets all the attention, the gluteus medius and minimus provide the stability that lets the glute max do its job better. That’s why it’s important to focus on all three, not just one.

Compound lifts hit them hard and heavy, but isolation exercises are necessary to train all glute functions and muscles. You can also load them in different ways: from a lengthened position (think RDL) and from a shortened position (think Hip Thrust).

Understanding those differences, rather than choosing sides in the great squat-versus-hip-thrust debate, is key to better glute training.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gQnMPHoDGEc

Each glute muscle has a different role, and understanding them will help you train them more effectively.

It’s the largest and most superficial of the three muscles, and it’s responsible for much of your backside’s size and shape. Although it’s best known for hip extension and external rotation, some lower fibers can assist with hip adduction depending on hip position, while the upper fibers assist with hip abduction.

The gluteus medius sits on the lateral side of your pelvis, partly beneath the gluteus maximus. Its primary job is hip abduction, but it also helps stabilize the pelvis. It also has different muscle fibers that perform different jobs. The anterior fibers assist with hip internal rotation, while the posterior fibers can contribute to external rotation.

The gluteus minimus is the smallest and deepest of the three, sitting underneath the glute medius. It assists with hip abduction and internal rotation while helping control the femur’s position within the hip joint. It also works with the glute medius to stabilize the pelvis when one foot leaves the ground.

The hip is a ball-and-socket joint that allows your hips to flex, extend, abduct, adduct, and rotate. But not everyone’s ball-and-socket joint is built the same way.

The depth and orientation of your hip socket, the angle of your femoral neck, and how much your femur rotates forward or backward vary from person to person. These structural differences influence exercise selection and positions.

Some squat with a narrow stance and toes pointed forward, while others go wider with toes pointed out. Your hip anatomy, mobility, strength, and limb length all influence what position works best for you. Adjusting your stance, foot position, and range of motion can help you find positions that load the glutes effectively and work with your anatomy.

Your glutes are among the body’s most powerful muscles, and paying attention to your backside pays off in more ways than one.

Glutes give you the horsepower to do the things you enjoy, from squatting to sprinting to other daily activities. The stronger they are, the more force they can produce, especially when you pair that strength with power training.

In many unilateral movements like walking, running, walking upstairs, and single-leg RDLs, smaller glute muscles control your lower-body position. Weakness can show up in a loss of balance, excessive wobbling in a single-leg stance, or your knee caving inward during squats and deadlifts. You don’t want any of that.

Your hips, knees, and lower back are teammates, and when one struggles, another may compensate. Weak glute med and glute min can cause knee valgus, which your knee ligaments don’t like. Weak hip extension strength or limited hip mobility forces the lower back to do a job it’s not designed for. Training the glutes for strength and mobility prevents this.

Almost every powerful lower-body movement involves the glutes.

During sprinting, the gluteus maximus drives powerful hip extension. When you cut, land, or change direction, all three glute muscles help control the hip and pelvis as your body absorbs and redirects force. The glutes also contribute to rotational movements, such as swinging a bat, throwing a punch, and a golf swing. Their ability to produce force and rotate helps link lower-body movement to upper-body power.

Here’s what your glutes need to grow bigger and stronger.

Compound exercises such as barbell squats, Romanian deadlifts, and barbell hip thrusts let the glutes produce force alongside the quads, hamstrings, and adductors, making them an excellent foundation for building strength and muscle.

Deep squats, front-foot elevated split squats, and deficit reverse lunges put a loaded stretch where you need it most. Because the hips are flexed and the glutes are lengthened, they can build greater muscle. Bonus points for using a controlled lowering phase.

Barbell hip thrusts, glute bridges, and cable kickback variations emphasize hip extension as the glutes approach their shortened position, given their smaller range of motion.

Neither approach is better, but both can help develop the glutes.

Hip abduction machines, lateral band walks, and side-lying hip raises train the gluteus medius, minimus, and the upper fibers of the gluteus maximus. These improve hip stability, allowing the glute max to work more effectively.

Seated band hip internal rotation, cable hip external rotation, and seated 90/90 hip rotations rotate the thigh within the hip joint while keeping the pelvis and lower back locked in. Rotational training supports hip stability, health, and more complete lower-body development.

The dreaded Bulgarian split squats, single-leg RDL’s, and step-ups train one leg at a time, improving hip stability. Unilateral exercises challenge the glutes to produce force and stabilize the pelvis, improving balance while strengthening imbalances between sides.

You don’t need 15 different glute exercises, but the right combination of movements that cover their various functions without turning every leg day into a marathon.

Start With Compound Bilateral And Unilateral Lifts

Compound lower-body lifts are the foundation of glute training because they let you go hard and heavy while other muscles join the party. But here’s an important distinction: Many compound lifts don’t isolate the glutes.

Compound lifts build strength and muscle, but moving more total weight doesn’t always mean the glutes get all the love. Squat depth, torso angle, hip position, and exercise technique influence how much work the glutes perform.

You need more than one type of hip-extension exercise because different movements challenge the glutes at different muscle lengths. Romanian deadlifts, full-range-of-motion squats, and front-foot elevated split squats load the glutes when they’re lengthened, while hip thrusts, glute bridges, and cable kickbacks emphasize tension closer to full hip extension, when the glutes are shorter.

Both can build size and strength, and each offers something the other doesn’t.

Don’t get caught up in the Team Squat versus Team Hip Thrust debate. Include exercises that challenge the glutes at both longer and shorter lengths, use a full range of motion you can control, and overload when you can.

Debates don’t build muscle. Training does.

Compound exercises train the glute med and mini, but direct hip-abduction exercises give them extra attention. When they’re stronger, your glute max can go to work unencumbered.

Broad jumps, sled pushes, hill sprints, and lateral bounds powerfully train the glutes and fire up your fast-twitch muscle fibers, which drive many of your gains. These exercises are great if you want your strength to carry over to athletic activities.

Your glutes can only work within the ranges your hips can access and control. Include half-kneeling hip flexor stretches with a posterior pelvic tilt, adductor rockbacks, 90/90 hip rotations, and prying squats in your warm-up to prepare for the work ahead.

The trick to training your glutes well is balancing heavy lifting, muscle-building work, and stability exercises while giving your backside enough time to recover. Here’s how to make it work.

Perform lower-body compound exercises, both bilateral and unilateral, with challenging weights. Maintain your technique and rest two to three minutes, or longer, between sets. Focus on progressive overload without sacrificing range of motion.

Again, use compound lower-body exercises that hit both lengthened and shortened positions, with a controlled eccentric contraction and full range of motion, training close to technical failure. Although muscle growth can happen across a wider rep range, this range balances load, effort, and fatigue.

Perform power movements early in your workout when you’re fresh, focus on maximum movement speed and quality, and rest 2 minutes or longer when needed to maintain explosiveness.

Hip abduction machines, cable abductions, and side-lying variations allow you to focus on the smaller glute muscles. Use controlled reps, avoid momentum, and progress the load.

Single-leg RDLs, step-ups, and Bulgarian split squats build strength while challenging stability. Only progress as your strength and balance improve.

Your weekly training volume should include all glute-focused exercises. Use the following table as a guideline, not a rule set in stone.

Some exercises train several qualities at once. A Bulgarian split squat challenges glute strength, muscle growth, and stability, but you don’t count the same set three times. Assign each set to its primary programming purpose (muscle/stability) when using the table.

For most lifters, two to three sessions per week is a good starting point.

Beginners can split their weekly work into two sessions, while intermediate lifters can use two or three. Experienced lifters focused on glute development will benefit from spreading the work over three sessions to maintain training quality.

Training your glutes isn’t rocket science, but you can make it harder than it needs to be. Here’s what to watch for and how to fix it.

Hip thrusts and bridge variations are excellent for building the glutes from the shortened position, but making them your only option misses opportunities to challenge the muscles at longer lengths and train hip abduction and stability.

The fix: Combine hip thrusts with RDLs, squats, split squats, and direct hip abduction exercises to cover more of the glutes’ functions.

It’s tempting to focus on exercises where you can really feel the squeeze, but muscle growth isn’t determined by how hard you can contract your glutes at lockout. RDLs, deep squats, and front-foot-elevated split squats challenge the glutes at longer muscle lengths, providing a different training stimulus.

The fix: Include at least one exercise that loads the glutes during greater hip flexion.

When chasing the squeeze or extra ROM in a hip thrust, deadlift, or RDL variation, some lifters extend their lower back instead of their glutes. Overarching your back at the top creates movement that doesn’t originate in the hips and shifts the focus away from where it belongs.

The fix: Keep your ribs over your hips, extend through your hips, and stop when you reach lockout.

The gluteus maximus gets the glory, but the smaller glute muscles help stabilize your pelvis, support the ball-and-socket movement, and produce hip abduction. Relying on compound lower-body exercises may leave these muscles undertrained.

The fix: Include band, cable, or machine hip abduction variations to give these smaller muscles the attention they deserve.

There’s one camp that says all you need for glutes is squats. Another camp says hip thrusts are all you need. Opinions run wild, so let’s separate fact from fiction.

Squats are fantastic for building glutes from a lengthened position, but the glutes need more than that, as they don’t challenge every glute function.

The truth: No one doubts squats are great for glutes, but training from a shortened position and direct hip-abduction exercises provide a different stimulus that can enhance muscle development.

Doing a set of hip thrusts tells you you’re engaging your glutes, but just because you “feel” it more doesn’t mean hip thrusts are better than squats for building muscle. Greater muscle activation during an exercise doesn’t necessarily translate into greater long-term muscle growth.

The truth: Research comparing hip thrusts and squats shows both build the glutes effectively, despite their different mechanics. For some, it comes down to personal preference.

Influencers with great glutes will scream from the rooftops that you can isolate and build an upper-glute shelf and a better lower-glute hamstring tie-in. But here’s some fact behind that fiction: The glute maximus has different fiber orientations that contribute to hip extension, abduction, adduction, and rotation.

The truth: Certain exercises and hip positions can shift the emphasis toward different glute regions, but you cannot turn off one area while training another. This is similar to what I explored in the upper- and lower-ab training myth.

If you walk up the stairs or sit down in slow motion after glute day, you might assume you’ve had the greatest glute workout ever. Hold your jeans.

The truth: Extreme muscle soreness usually signals a new training stimulus or heavy eccentric loading, and it isn’t a reliable measure of muscle gain.

Adjust the loads, sets, reps, and exercise variations to match your experience and recovery. Perform them as standalone sessions or fit them into your existing program.

Rest periods: Rest two to three minutes after each superset and 90 seconds between exercises.

Progressive overload: When you reach the upper end of a rep range with clean technique, increase the load slightly.

Manage weekly volume: The full-body workout includes nine glute-focused resistance sets, while the lower-body workout includes 11. Keep that in mind when combining these into your current routine or performing both in the same week.

People rap about and admire the glutes, but they’re the engine that makes the body roar in and out of the gym.

Building stronger, more muscular glutes takes more than hip thrusts and band booty burners. Train the glute max through all its functions, give the med and mini some love, and combine exercises that challenge your backside in lengthened and shortened positions. Include unilateral training, progressive overload, and adequate rest and recovery, and your jeans will thank you.

One last thing. Turn around and admire your handy work.

Liam Fitzgerald, a popular online coach and fitness influencer has passed away at just 29 years of age after injuries sustained during a fatal motorcycle accident. Tributes have poured in for the star, and his family have hailed him as an inspirational figure.

Fitzgerald, who was born in Evansville, Wisconsin, and was a social media influencer and OnlyFans creator, died on October 30, per announcement by his girlfriend Jamie Lyn Rinaldi. “It is with the heaviest heart that I share the devastating news that Liam passed away following a motorcycle accident on October 30th at approximately 2 AM,” she wrote via Instagram. “He suffered severe injuries, and despite the efforts of those who tried desperately to save him, they were unable to bring him back. There are no words to describe the heartbreak of this loss.”

Fitzgerald was an athlete before becoming an influencer and after a move to Washington state, his teenage years were highly active. Fitzgerald played football as a quarterback for the Camas Papermakers, skateboarded, and developed a love of working out. He later relocated to Arizona and finally settled in Miami, Florida, where he built an Instagram base of more than one million followers by sharing his fitness, fashion, and lifestyle advice.

Fitzgerald also collaborated with well known brands such as YoungLA, who posted a tribute to the star via its official Instagram account. “He brought an incredible energy, joy, and excitement to every shoot, making every moment that much more special,” read the statement. “His presence will be deeply missed, and we are grateful to have had the opportunity to work alongside him.”

The influencer’s family has also spoken about Fitzgerald’s struggles with alcohol. “This is shared in the hope that his story reaches someone who needs it,” read a statement. “He wasn’t perfect and never pretended to be. But he always strived to grow and do better. He had dreams, ambitions, and so much more life to live. He had just turned 29. So many places to see, memories to make, and people to love. His life was tragically cut short in a motorcycle accident, leaving behind a heartbreak that words will never be able to describe.”

It’s official, 20-year-old Kimi Antonelli has secured his spot as the youngest F1 Champion in history after just two seasons, but while the dedicated Mercedes driver has been relentless on the track, the speedy Italian has also stayed active outside of his car. Here’s why the history maker’s appetite for adventure is the reason that he never stays still, and how a smart approach to staying active benefits both body and mind.

Kimi Antonelli’s third place in Mexico City on November 1 meant that he’d earned enough points to stave off all other drivers to complete the season as champion, but this overnight success is the result of a mature approach to staying sharp. “I try to do things that keep me active, but won’t tire me out,” explained Antonelli during a recent and telling interview with GQ. “It’s all a way to release mental stress, to just relax and enjoy. I try to do these activities as much as possible because in sports, the mental [part] is basically what does everything.”

The activities that Antonelli spoke of include race related training such as simulators, go-karts, and operating remote controlled cars, but he’s also a keen proponent of padel. Not only has the young upstart played against fellow Mercedes drivers like George Russell, but he’s even been known to stroke the ball from the deck of a super yacht from time to time.

Antonelli’s fuel for dominating F1 was on show early, as he transitioned from Formula 2 and continued his approach to “hard” training, sharing that a day of working out included “An early morning swim, neck training at lunch, and an afternoon bike ride.”

The inspirational Italian is also hot with the hoops, and in a recent Instagram Reel revealed that he can make a basket from an impressive distance, all while standing on one leg!

While Antonelli’s love of fun activities helps him keep a positive mindset as he works towards pole position, science has also shown that becoming skilled in a variety of sporting activities can only help with his day job. Activities such as shooting baskets, stroking the Padel ball, and other loves such as surfing, no doubt boost his reaction times. In fact, a scientific study in 2023 confirmed that reaction training (they used flashing lights as the stimuli) induced beneficial effects on physiological and cognitive performance.

At just 20 years of age, Kimi Antonelli has the world at his highly successful feet. So, what’s next? “Right now, my main goal is to give everything to F1, but in my normal life, I want to be successful, too,” he revealed to GQ. “I want to be efficient, and in 20 to 30 years’ time, when I won’t be racing anymore, I want to still do something that keeps me active. Because once you finish, it’s easy to do nothing after working hard for so many years. I want to be successful outside of racing.”

With an attitude like Antonelli’s, the journey is far from over.

#8638. The Arizona Experiment!

The thing that drew me to early retirement is freedom, and that’s still the best part of it.

Back in 2005, the primary reason for this freedom-seeking was being able to devote my best hours to being a Dad – I had a feeling my career in tech would be too demanding to sustain once the full-time job of raising children kicked in.

Eighteen years later, wow has that guess ever turned out to be right. Early retirement has proved to be the most amazing, worthwhile adventure and it’s still just getting started. It was an astonishing thirteen years ago that I wrote to you about Little MM starting kindergarten, and now he’s done with high school.

It has given me the space to enjoy so many new experiences, working hard and playing hard sometimes, but also slowing things way down when necessary, to deal with and grow through some real hardships.

But now, with that child-raising phase finally almost done, I’m cashing in a few of those Freedom Chips for a particularly big change: moving to a warm sunny place for the winter to try out a new life in the walkable, bikeable, car-free community you’ve probably heard me raving about in the past: Culdesac Tempe.

So on the first of December I’ll be packing up the essential clothes, tools and gadgets, and throwing my very best mountain bike onto the Model Y to make the epic road trip across the mountains. Just in time to escape the incoming Colorado winter. And my son will be joining me for the trip!

Looking for updates? I have added a separate tracker page here.

We’ve booked ourselves a spacious two bedroom apartment there, for four full months. Little MM will be roughly alternating his months between Arizona and Colorado so he can still have time with both parents, while I’ll be there the whole time.

A big part of the fun is that this will force me to invent a whole new life for myself, away from the easy comforts of the big community and plentiful construction sites that keep me so busy here.  It will be both a big change and a significant challenge, which is exactly what all of us need on a regular basis to keep life full of meaning and joy.

The exact details are still in the works, and I’d love to hear your ideas and feedback (see the “get in touch” note below. But here’s what I’ve got so far:

Okay, you’re onto me. If I’m going to go to the trouble of typing shit into the computer and sharing it with you, there’s usually a purpose behind it other than just journaling my own personal life, and this another one of those cases.

First of all, there are the first-layer selfish goals: I want to have the best winter ever, meet a bunch of smart new people, and I also want Culdesac to be a huge success so they will build more neighborhoods like this around the country and set an example that permanently improves the way US cities build and expand themselves in the future.

But even if you don’t care about all that, I also want to use this as a little statement about trying deliberate life changes.

By throwing myself into a new community which aligns so nicely with my own values, I hope to serve as a reminder that maybe you might want to try the same thing. Or just try anything new.

In a comfortable, prosperous country like ours, some of the built in tendencies of Human nature tend to work against us, saying,

“Hey – I’ve noticed we have plenty of food and reasonable shelter and that’s good enough. So let’s just double down on the Netflix, comfort foods, and occasional luxury purchases and that will keep us safe.”

Instead, I want you to set your life treadmill to just a bit of a steeper, healthier incline setting.

That means questioning the status quo and doing your best to keep at least one little experiment on the go in the background. Maybe that means forcing yourself to move to a better place, or taking steps towards getting a new job that gives you a better work-life balance.

The biggest move I ever made was leaving family and friends and my old job behind to move to the US, alone, at age 24. Looking back, I’m shocked I had the courage (and the organizational skills) to pull that off back then. I’ve become older and a bit slower, and so comfortable that it’s hard to imagine doing something so bold now.

But even today 24 years later, I thank my past self every single day for doing it. My present life is an incredibly different and better thing because of that past bit of courage.

The spirit of positive experimentation might also mean starting to challenge your body more regularly – giving it harder work and exposing it to a wider swath of temperatures and movements. Or joining new Meetup groups to expand your circle of friends and experiences.

It doesn’t really matter exactly what you do, as long as you point your feet in what feels like a good direction and just start moving. Create some purposeful change, which will surely feel a bit difficult, simply because change is hard. And hard things are good.

Future Arizona Neighbors: I’ll see you in four weeks!

Further reading: I’ve been reading books, doing life experiments, and writing about the value of strategic hardship for a while now. But the latest is a book called Dopamine Nation by the talented psychiatrist/author named Dr. Anna Lembke.

To summarize: your brain creates a baseline for happiness based on the HARDEST thing you do, and then compares everything else to that. So if you do hard things, life in general seems fantastic because of this perspective. If you eliminate all hardship, suddenly even the pleasures of life seem bland, and you live a spoiled and unmotivated life.

I recently read that book after hearing the author interviewed by both Joe Rogan and Andrew Huberman. It gave me a new perspective on motivation and “happiness”, and closed the loop on these ideas as so practically described by MMM. Satisfaction, contentment, and motivation come to us by way of the “struggle” and the the effort of dealing with and facing challenging situations of all sorts – physical, emotional, and mental. Feeding our desires constantly – eating, entertainment, alcohol, drugs, shopping, etc. – only serve to make us less and less happy and more and more depressed. Eliminating our cravings and desires, while pursuing intentional hardships to keep us fit, sharp, and strong, ultimates results in a more satisfying state of mind and a fulfilling sense of wellbeing. It all comes together with the MMM philosophy of living a simple, frugal, productive, and healthy lifestyle.

But I do like to share a general message, because divorce is such a common thing yet it is widely associated with shame and blame: it is OKAY if it’s right for you. It’s not a failure or a negative, selfish choice. And more people need to get over the fear of making changes like that in their lives, once they have done their best to think it through. And more people need to be nice about it as they go through the process.

HEY! Look at that! All my worlds are colliding!

I’m a fellow Canadian (Newfoundlander to be precise) who’s been reading your blog from the very beginning. Mostly it’s a case of “preaching to the converted”.

I’ve been spending winters in Arizona for the last 10 years because my partner (also from Newfoundland) lives in Chandler. And literally, no joke, the first item that I have written down on my list of things to do in Arizona this coming winter is “go check out Cul De Sac”.

Maybe if I go and wander around there, I’ll spot your facial hair

I don’t know if it’s weird to say this, but I’d be up for a coffee or a bike ride or some hang time or whatever if you feel so inclined. It would definitely be the weirdest way that I’ve ever made a friend. In a good way.

Anyway, obviously the desert has lots of beautiful hikes and bike rides. But do yourself a favour (note the “u” in favour LoL) and go check out The Desert Botanical Gardens. It’s one of the absolute gems in The Valley. It can sometimes have lots of tourists there … particularly us Canucks. But it’s for good reason. It is spectacular. And they have lots of cool events there too. We take all our visitors there. And if you’re so inclined, the library offers free passes to DBG and lots of other local attractions too.

(1) The Musical Instrument Museum is pretty huge and unique

(2) The drive out to Tortilla Flats is really beautiful. It literally is an old stage coach trail that was turned into a twisty 2 lane highway.  And you can go boating or kayaking in Canyon lake, which is pretty sweet.

(3) Sedona is obviously one of the most gorgeous places in the US and a reasonably short drive. If you’re going to go to the Grand Canyon from Sedona (or even if you’re just going to Flagstaff), there’s this fabulous older highway called 89A that takes you to Flagstaff. It’s so much more fun than taking the freeway.

(4) There are oodles and oodles of free Disc Golf courses (my new obsession and the price is right)

(5) South Mountain has a thing called “Silent Sunday” where they close the mountain to cars. So you can ride your bike up (obviously challenging) but then down (woo hoo!)

(6) There’s a cool thing downtown called “First Friday Art Walk” every month. Google it.

(7) Most importantly, my favourite place to ride my bike is in the Northern part of The McDowell Sonoran Preserve. Specifically, I like the trail called “The Long Way Around”. It’s just the right length (around 25 km). The ground is very beginner friendly. In fact, I have a hybrid, not a mountain bike and it does fine. But the trail still has lots of ups and downs and twists and turns, so it’s a blast. So much so, that the first time I rode there, I was giggling like a kid, even though I’m 55. It’s as easy or hard as you want it to be, based on how fast you go. And also it’s one of the nicest parks in the area.

(8) Taliesin West is super cool. Particularly if you get a good guide. It was Frank Lloyd Wright’s personal project. His winter home. So he was free to do whatever crazy things he could dream up, without having to account to a client. The handyman in you will love it!

I could go on, but that’s off the top of my head.

One last note. If you wear something Canadian; like for example, I wear a CBC logo on my hat or my partner wears something from the Leafs … a zillion snowbird Canadians will approach you and ask what part of Canada you’re from.

Anyway, here’s to a great time in Arizona.

The best workaround for Delta dynamic pricing on premium cabins

Here's the insight that changes everything: Delta prices its own award seats dynamically, which means when you search Delta.com for a SkyMiles redemption, you're at the mercy of an algorithm that reads demand, load factors, and booking timing. A Delta One Suite that costs 50,000 SkyMiles one week might jump to 120,000 or even 250,000 SkyMiles the next. It's unpredictable, often punishing, and fundamentally unfair to the loyal customer who saved up miles expecting consistency.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club doesn't play by those rules.

Virgin Atlantic is a Delta SkyTeam partner, which means Flying Club members can book seats on Delta-operated flights using their Virgin Atlantic miles. But critically — and this is the entire mechanism — Virgin Atlantic prices Delta award seats on a fixed award chart, not Delta's dynamic pricing system. That chart currently prices Delta One (business class) on transcon routes like JFK–LAX at 50,000 miles one-way. No matter what Delta's algorithm is doing that day, your Virgin Atlantic redemption rate stays fixed.

This is a classic pricing inefficiency created by partner award charts lagging behind airline pricing strategies. Delta has every incentive to raise its own SkyMiles pricing — it captures more revenue from its own loyalty currency. But Delta has far less control over what a partner program charges to access its seats. Virgin Atlantic's award chart is, in effect, a door into Delta inventory that bypasses Delta's own toll booth.

The points you need to fund this redemption are almost certainly already sitting in currencies you have or can easily earn:

For a redemption this valuable, the 1:1 instant transfers from Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt are your primary path. You transfer exactly what you need, the miles appear in your Flying Club account immediately, and you book. No waiting, no uncertainty.

Virgin Atlantic has a reputation for imposing high fuel surcharges on its own operated flights — and that reputation is well-earned. But here's the critical nuance: surcharges do NOT apply to partner awards. When you book a Delta-operated flight through Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, you pay only the standard carrier-imposed taxes and fees, which are minimal on domestic U.S. routes. On JFK–LAX, expect to pay roughly $5–$15 in taxes. That's it. The surcharge concern that makes some people avoid Virgin Atlantic entirely simply doesn't apply here.

Flying Club miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. Keep your account active with at least one earning or redemption activity every three years, and your miles will remain intact indefinitely. This is a very traveler-friendly policy compared to programs with hard expiration dates.

Free calculator shows when you could reach financial independence — plus a savings rate tracker, expense audit, and more.

Do NOT start at Virgin Atlantic's website — their search tool for partner awards is limited. Instead, go directly to delta.com and search for your desired route (e.g., JFK → LAX) in the date range you're targeting. Select "Use miles" as your payment method and filter by Business class. You're not booking here — you're prospecting.

What you're looking for: Delta One availability showing in the results. When you see it, note the exact flight number, date, and departure time. Delta.com will show you the SkyMiles price (which will be high under dynamic pricing), but ignore that number entirely. You just need to confirm the seat exists.

You need 50,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles per person. Before transferring anything, confirm which flexible points currency you're working with:

All transfer at 1:1 instantly. If you're using Marriott Bonvoy points, the ratio is 3:1 (so 150,000 Bonvoy points = 50,000 Flying Club miles), and transfers take 1–5 days.

Once you've confirmed availability on a specific flight, transfer your points. Use the transfer portal within your credit card program's website (Chase, Amex, Citi, or Bilt). You'll need your Flying Club membership number — create a free account at virginatlantic.com/us/en/flying-club if you don't have one.

For Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt transfers: miles appear instantly in your Flying Club account. Confirm the balance before proceeding.

Critical warning: Do not transfer points until you've verbally confirmed availability with a Virgin Atlantic agent (Step 4). Points transfers are irreversible.

This is a phone booking, not an online booking. Call Virgin Atlantic Flying Club at 1-800-365-9500. Have your flight details ready:

Ask the agent to confirm that Delta One award availability exists on your chosen flight before you transfer points. If they confirm it, then transfer and call back — or ask to be placed on a brief hold while you complete the transfer (instant transfers make this possible).

Once your miles are transferred and the agent has confirmed availability, they'll complete the booking. You'll pay only standard carrier taxes and fees — expect roughly $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. route. You'll receive a Virgin Atlantic booking confirmation, but your ticket will show Delta as the operating carrier.

Virgin Atlantic can book Delta awards up to 331 days in advance. For the best seat selection and availability, aim to search within that window as early as possible.

Delta SkyMiles uses fully dynamic pricing with no published award chart, meaning business class awards can range from 80,000 to 500,000 SkyMiles for the same route depending on demand. Virgin Atlantic, as a Delta joint venture partner, maintains a fixed award chart for Delta-operated flights — creating a massive pricing arbitrage. A JFK-to-London Delta One Suite that Delta prices at 350,000 SkyMiles can often be booked through Virgin for 47,500 Flying Club miles. Both programs see the same award inventory, but Virgin prices it using their distance-based chart instead of Delta's demand-based algorithm. Since Virgin Atlantic's Flying Club accepts 1:1 transfers from Chase, Amex, Capital One, Citi, and Bilt, you can earn these miles through credit card spending without ever flying Virgin Atlantic.

Let's walk through a real example so the numbers become concrete.

The Route: New York JFK → Los Angeles LAX The Aircraft: Airbus A350-900 The Cabin: Delta One Suites

Pull up Delta.com on a typical travel date and you'll find Delta One Suites on this route priced anywhere from $2,500 for a off-peak weekday to $5,000–$6,000 during peak summer weekends or holiday travel. Let's use a realistic midpoint of $3,500 — a completely standard price for business class on one of America's most competitive routes.

If you earned those 50,000 points via a Chase Sapphire Reserve welcome bonus (currently 60,000 points) and some organic spend, your real cost to acquire the points was a small fraction of the flight's retail value.

You check in at JFK's Terminal 4 with Delta status access or a Priority Pass card in hand, clearing into the Delta Sky Club or the premium Centurion Lounge (if you carry the Amex Platinum). Then you board the A350-900 and find your suite.

The five-hour flight from New York to Los Angeles becomes an experience rather than a commute. You arrive rested, full, and having spent roughly $11 out of pocket on a seat your fellow passengers paid $3,500 for. That gap — that's the ChooseFI travel rewards mindset in action.

Virgin Atlantic can book Delta awards up to 331 days in advance. Delta One availability on high-demand routes like JFK–LAX is not unlimited — it's released in waves and often fills quickly for peak dates. Set a calendar reminder to search exactly 331 days before your target travel date. This is especially important for holiday travel, summer weekends, and any dates where you have a hard deadline.

Since transfers from Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt are instant, you can do a same-call transfer — confirm availability with the agent, ask them to hold for a moment, transfer your points in a separate browser tab, and confirm with the agent that the miles have landed. This eliminates the risk of availability disappearing between your transfer and your booking attempt.

While this sweet spot is available year-round, Delta One availability is generally better on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday departures when leisure demand is lower. If your travel dates are flexible, searching across a week of dates will often surface better availability on midweek flights.

Virgin Atlantic's award chart has high fuel surcharges on Virgin Atlantic-operated flights. This guide is specifically about Delta-operated flights. Never confuse the two. When you call to book, confirm the operating carrier is Delta. The surcharge-free benefit applies only to partner awards.

Points transfers are irreversible. A common and painful mistake is transferring points to Flying Club only to discover the specific flight you wanted has no award availability. Always confirm availability verbally with a Flying Club agent before initiating any transfer.

The most efficient path to 50,000 points is a single credit card welcome bonus. The Chase Sapphire Preferred or Chase Sapphire Reserve both offer welcome bonuses that can fully fund this redemption — and both transfer to Virgin Atlantic at 1:1 instantly. Alternatively, the Amex Gold Card or Platinum Card welcome bonuses work equally well via Amex's instant transfer path.

Flying Club miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. A simple fix: make a small earning transaction (even a hotel stay or car rental through their partners) at least once every three years.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

This redemption is ideal for couples and solo travelers who want a genuinely luxurious experience on one of America's premier transcontinental routes and are comfortable with a moderate amount of booking complexity — primarily a phone call to Virgin Atlantic.

Minimum points needed: 50,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles per person (100,000 for two). These are most efficiently sourced via a single credit card welcome bonus.

For the FI-minded traveler who has earned a moderate points balance and wants to experience premium cabin travel on a meaningful domestic route, this is a standout use of currency. The 5–12 CPP range makes it one of the most efficient domestic business class redemptions available.

This redemption is rated **moderate** — not because any individual step is technically complex, but because it requires coordinating two separate systems (Delta.com for availability searching and Virgin Atlantic by phone for booking) and making an irreversible transfer decision under some time pressure. **What makes it moderately challenging:** 1. **Availability is the main hurdle.** Delta One award inventory released to partners is limited, particularly on peak dates. You won't always find seats when you want them, and the 331-day booking window means planning further ahead than most travelers are accustomed to. 2. **The booking requires a phone call.** There's no self-service online booking for Virgin Atlantic partner awards. Some travelers find this intimidating; in practice, Flying Club agents are helpful and accustomed to partner award bookings. 3. **The transfer-before-booking sequence requires discipline.** The rule is: confirm first, transfer second. Getting that order wrong is an expensive mistake. **Three tips to make this easier:** - **Use Delta.com as your search engine.** It shows real-time award availability far more reliably than third-party tools for Delta-operated flights. - **Call Virgin Atlantic during off-peak hours** (early morning Eastern time tends to mean shorter hold times and more patient agents). - **Have your flight details written down** before you call — flight number, date, origin, destination, and Flying Club number. A prepared caller gets a faster, smoother booking. If you've ever transferred points to an airline program and called to book an award, this process will feel completely familiar. If this is your first partner award booking, treat it as a learning experience — the 5–12 CPP reward on the other side is well worth one phone call.

Log into your Delta SkyMiles account and search for one-way business class (Delta One) award flights. Filter for nonstop flights on the A350-900, which is the aircraft with Delta One Suites. Note the dates that show availability — this is the same inventory Virgin can book.

If you do not already have a Virgin Atlantic Flying Club account, create one at virginatlantic.com. You need an active account to receive transferred miles and to reference when calling to book.

Transfer the required miles from your preferred partner: Chase Ultimate Rewards (instant transfer), Amex Membership Rewards (typically 1-2 business days), Capital One (1-2 days), Citi ThankYou (instant to 24 hours), or Bilt (1-2 days). Always confirm availability before transferring.

Call Virgin Atlantic Flying Club at their US number. Provide the specific flight number, date, and route you found on delta.com. The agent will search for the same availability and quote the mileage cost from Virgin's fixed award chart. Confirm the booking and pay taxes and fees.

Virgin Atlantic's fixed award chart prices Delta One flights based on distance. Transatlantic routes (US to Europe) typically cost 47,500 to 60,000 Virgin miles one-way in business class. Transpacific routes cost more, around 60,000 to 80,000 miles. Compare this to Delta SkyMiles, which can charge 200,000 to 500,000 miles for the same seats.

No. As of 2026, Virgin Atlantic does not support online booking for Delta partner awards. You must call Virgin Atlantic's Flying Club phone line to book. Search for availability on delta.com first, then call with the specific flight details. The call typically takes 10-15 minutes.

Delta One is the business class cabin available on multiple aircraft types with lie-flat seats but no closing door. Delta One Suites are only on the A350-900 and feature a fully enclosed suite with a closing door, a wider seat, and a more private experience. When booking, verify the aircraft type is A350-900 to ensure you get the Suite product.

Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers to Virgin Atlantic are instant. Citi ThankYou points are also fast, typically completing within minutes to 24 hours. Amex Membership Rewards and Bilt usually take 1-2 business days. Capital One transfers take 1-2 days as well. If you find availability and need to book quickly, Chase is the best source.

Booking Delta One Suites through Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is the definitive workaround for Delta's punishing dynamic pricing. Paying 50,000 transferable points for a seat that Delta prices at 350,000 SkyMiles is one of the largest arbitrage opportunities in travel rewards. The fully enclosed suite with a closing door is the best international business class product any US carrier offers. Yes, you need to call to book — but that 15-minute phone call saves you 300,000 miles. Build your transferable points balances with Chase, Amex, or Bilt, search delta.com for A350 availability, and let Virgin Atlantic's fixed award chart do the rest.

#8633. Why the Spanish Squat Can Help Build Quads without Using a Barbell

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

The traditional back squat has long been the staple of those who want to crush their quads, but standing under a heavy barbell is not for everyone. Mature gym goers, or anyone with mobility issues, may find that the downward force of carrying a heavy bar across the shoulders leads to stress on the spine. Fortunately, IFBB Pro and physique transformation coach, Tanya Johansen swears by the Spanish squat.

“Try a Spanish squat,” recommends the Bikini Pro competitor. “It fries your quads… when done correctly.”

The Spanish squat is a popular movement utilized for rehabbing the knees, but it also pounds the quadriceps, providing the perfect environment for muscle growth. To try it for yourself, stand in front of a cable station or power rack and anchor a resistance band around the support, looping around the back of your knees. You can stand inside a single loop, or loop the band around each knee, as demonstrated by Johansen.

Next, move back a little to make sure there is tension on the band. Now, you should be able to squat by sitting back with the band keeping you upright. Keep your shins vertical, and place emphasis on the quads as you lift and lower your body.  “Band behind your knees, sit back into it, stay tall, let your knees come forward,” summarized the coach, who specializes in physiques that are over 40.

Because there is no barbell compressing your body, the Spanish squat can be executed without overloading the back and knee joints. The quads can still be worked hard with no additional weight, and for those looking to improve their range of mobility, Spanish squats are awesome for building knee strength because they rehab the patellar and its related tendons.

“Over 40? Even better reason,” advises the coach of the Spanish squat. “You don’t need a heavy bar on your back to grow your legs. Forget heavy. Make the muscle do the work.”  And, for those who use the barbell as a crux for their ego, this IFBB Pro has some real talk. “You’re not in there to impress anyone,” she explained. “You’re in there to make sure your quads earn it.”

To make this move more challenging, you can bring in an isometric hold at the top of the squat, pausing before descending back down. You can also slow down the lowering phase for additional time under tension. Aim for 3 sets of 8 to 12 reps.

“It’s not the weight. It’s the work,” concluded Johansen, who’s own physique is proof positive that training smart can bring serious progress.

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

As we know, protein is a crucial part of healthy eating and building muscle. Without adequate daily protein, the chances of packing on all the muscle you want are slim.

While the ideal amount of protein will vary from individual to individual, it’s a good idea to spread out your intake of this crucial macro throughout the day to make it easier to get all that you need. Trying to pack 100 grams of protein into a single meal is never a wise move. Who ever said that getting your fill of protein needs to stop at dinner? The protein spread can (and should) include dessert. With a little effort and know-how, you can give your ab-friendly sweat treats a protein boost without making them taste all healthy and what-not. Using the right ingredients, it’s certainly possible to make a dessert that gives you 10 grams or more of protein, which is significant in your daily pursuit to get enough. And, sure, you could just blend together a post-dinner protein shake, but where’s the fun in that?

Higher-protein desserts, be it for an end-of-day treat or part of a game day spread, can help you reach your goals for this clutch macronutrient. Here’s how to make some treats that do much more than satisfy a sweet tooth. Everything in moderation, right?

Certain ingredients can give your treats a protein boost. So if you’re looking for a dessert that’ll help you build muscle, include any of these protein heroes.

Protein Powder: Good for much more than your post-gym recovery shakes, versatile protein powder can be used in a huge variety of dessert recipes, both cooked and uncooked. For baking, it can replace some of the flour in a recipe. But it’s best to use plant-based protein powders in baking recipes like muffins and cakes as they give a much better texture than powders made from whey.

Peanut Butter Powder: This is the best thing to add nutty taste to dessert that you probably aren’t using. Peanut butter powder is made by pressing roasted peanuts to remove most of their natural oils, then grinding the defatted peanuts into a fine powder. This process significantly reduces the fat and calorie content compared to peanut butter, and results in a more protein-dense product. A good buy is Naked Nutrition Peanut Butter Powder.

Greek Yogurt: Enhance the protein content of your desserts by using Greek yogurt or Skyr instead of regular yogurt in recipes. It’s an easy substitution that packs an extra protein punch with minimal change to the flavor or texture.

Chia Seeds: Chia seeds offer four grams of protein in just two tablespoons —and they help create a creamy pudding that will be a delicious high-protein dessert (or breakfast).

These (mostly) healthy high protein desserts are sure to satisfy and will help ramp up your protein intake throughout the day.

In a blender or food processor, blend together the cottage cheese, maple syrup and vanilla until smooth. Transfer to a mixing bowl and stir in the oat flour, peanut butter powder, and cocoa powder until well incorporated. Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator. It should stay fresh for up to one week.

This protein-heavy, sweet bread is great for breakfast, dessert, or a snack. Sweet potato provides natural sweetness, while peanut butter adds richness and some additional protein to each slice. It’s great with a generous smear of cream cheese. Be sure to use a plant-based protein powder instead of whey for better texture.

Preheat oven to 350°F. Line a standard-sized loaf pan with parchment paper or use a non-stick silicone loaf pan.

In a large bowl, mix together flour, protein powder, baking powder, baking soda, cinnamon, and salt. In a separate bowl, whisk together sweet potato, peanut butter, milk, maple syrup, and vanilla. Add wet ingredients to bowl with dry ingredients and mix gently until everything is moist. Pour batter into pan and smooth the surface with a spatula. Sprinkle on peanuts and press them down lightly to adhere.

Bake for 40 minutes, or until a toothpick inserted into the center of the loaf comes out mostly clean. Allow loaf to cool in pan for 10 minutes before cooling the loaf further on a metal rack.

Here’s how to give your dessert a taste of the tropics. The superpower of chia seeds is that they soak up liquid like a sponge, which produces a pudding-like texture. This is also a stand-out make-ahead breakfast option. Greek yogurt adds plenty of protein, but you can go bigger on this macro by also blending in your favorite protein powder.

Place mango, milk, yogurt, honey, lime juice, lime zest, ginger and a pinch of salt in a blender and blend until smooth. Divide among 2 jars. Add half of the chia seeds to each jar and stir to combine. Sprinkle on almonds or pistachios. Seal shut and chill for at least 3 hours and up to 3 days.

Avocado gives these ice cream-like frozen cups a fudgy consistency and plenty of good nutrition. Protein powder adds a solid amount of the muscle-making macro, bananas are here for some natural sweetness, and cayenne provides as surprising spicy kick. Only if all ice cream could be this good for you and still taste great.

Place bananas, avocado flesh, nut butter, protein powder, maple syrup or honey, cocoa powder, cinnamon, cayenne, and a pinch of salt in a blender or food processor container and process until smooth.

Line muffin pan with 8 paper liners. (You can skip this step if using silicone muffin cups). Scoop banana batter into muffin cups. Sprinkle on flaky salt if using. Place tray in the freezer and freeze for at least 2 hours, or until solid. Unmold fudge pucks and store in the freezer in an airtight container until ready to serve. When ready to serve, leave fudge pucks out at room temperature for a few minutes to soften slightly.

#8625. How To Afford a House These Days

The other day, an MMM reader stopped by and left the following comment on one of my older posts about the principles of FIRE:

“While I still find some of MMM’s advice relevant, it seems like every FI blogger out there worked in tech 20 years ago, pulled down a 6 figure salary and bought a house for a bag of potatoes before 2019.

I wasn’t smart enough to find FI when I was young so I sometimes feel like a lot of their advice is not going to help me or others who don’t already own a home and don’t have six- figure salaries in this post-pandemic world.

A lot of the ideas given to young folks are “house hack” “buy a fixer upper” but that is still out of reach and/or complex to navigate with current prices and interest rates. Most townships around me do not want you to chop a house up into ADU’s or multiple units. My cousin owns 60 acres of land but he is not allowed to live on a trailer on that land.

I don’t know what the next generation of FI bloggers will offer, perhaps they are already out there and I just don’t know who they are, but I’d like to hear from them.”–

As with every critique of our ideas, I thought about this comment for a while. Tried to determine if there were any Principles of Mustachianism that were genuinely going obsolete, versus the more common side effects of Complainypants and/or Excuse-itis, two afflictions which have been weighing down our critics since the beginning.

After all, this isn’t the first time FIRE has gone obsolete. Over my retirement I’ve seen it:

Our commenter focuses on two things: the solid salaries of tech workers, and the major increases in house prices (and interest rates) in the most recent four years.

The first one — high salaries in general – is still a factor and I don’t expect that to change. Some jobs just pay more than others, and there’s a lot you can do to increase your income and switch jobs, and I’m all for it. However, ever-increasing income is not my usual focus here on MMM, because I have seen first hand that most people can waste almost any amount of income and still have very little to show for it.

In fact, the very existence of software engineers and doctors and other high earners who are my age and still feeling financial stress is proof of this: it’s mathematically impossible to earn so much for almost 30 years and not have an absolute shit-ton saved, unless you are also spending an absolute shit-ton of money the whole time.

So instead, we focus on how to streamline your spending and live joyfully and efficiently without compromise. We focus on reducing waste, while maintaining or even increasing all of the other benefits that come from spending money more purposefully. These skills are essential even for the highest earners, but they become even more valuable as you move down the income ladder.

So now for the second issue: housing. Does the state of housing here in 2024 screw up the whole FIRE plan?

As with any question, let’s start by looking at the data: how much have US house prices actually risen – adjusted for inflation – since 2019?

It turns out that our own St. Louis Fed makes this extremely useful  information available here.

So there’s our answer: houses “feel” about 25% more expensive right now than they did at the start of 2019 relative to the average salary and the price of everything else. Although interestingly enough,  they are only up about 10% since the last peak in early 2006, a full eighteen years ago! So housing is a blow, but not a FIRE-extinguishing one.

However, this nationwide data masks some much bigger increases in certain popular cities, including my own: Plain old Longmont Colorado now sports a hilariously high $540,000 median home price. So houses are about triple the price they were when I started writing in 2011, which means they’ve risen much faster than the average salary. Which means houses are much further out of reach for the average person in my area.

The solution to this is the same as most other problems: to stop thinking in the way our culture likes to train us (as a victim of outside forces beyond our control) and go back to thinking like a Mustachian.

Houses are just like any other manufactured product, and as such they come at a wide variety of prices, subject to supply and demand.

And just because you happen to live in a certain place (even if you were born and raised there), doesn’t mean you’ll automatically be able to afford to buy a house there. Just as a baby born upon the Apple campus in Cupertino today doesn’t automatically get a new iPhone Pro Max every year.

With every purchasing decision, you need to go through the same series of choices:

So when it comes to houses, you run the numbers, then decide between renting or buying or house hacking. You might start by doing the analysis right in your own city, but also keep in mind that there are lots of other cities and even countries in the world, and there are happy people living in all of them.

But Wait: I don’t want to move to a whole new place!

At this point, people get defensive. We all have ties to our current location, and the stronger the ties the more difficult it becomes to consider moving.

But there’s a difference between genuine, positive bonds to a place and just plain old fear of change. So it’s my job to at least make you question your assumptions, because not doing so is what got you where you are, and it’s also what got our country where it is.

And on a country-wide basis,  I notice that our general fear of relocating creates a very irrational pattern of house prices. They are ridiculously high in some places and ridiculously cheap in others. There does seem to be a general correlation between niceness and cost, but not a perfect one (especially since everyone has their own definition of “nice”)

I moved to Longmont in 2005 because it met our young family’s needs at the time, at the right price with homes about $200,000. Today, at the $540,000 price level (houses average about $450 per interior square foot) it has to compete with a much broader range of cities which offer nicer amenities at equal or lower prices.

Let’s do a hypothetical search using another amazing tool: FRED’s list of the top 1000 metro areas with price per square foot, and plot some of them based on my own judgment of their desirability:

I’m biased towards Colorado because I have so many ties there, and I also highly prioritize sunny climates. My chart suggests that if I wanted to save money, I might start looking around in Albuquerque, whereas Denver would give me a nicer life in the same price range as my current city of Longmont. And if I were willing to spend even more on housing to live somewhere even nicer, I should suck it up and move to Boulder.

Just for fun, I pulled the data from that same FRED website into a separate google spreadsheet (which I’ll share here) and sorted it by cost per square foot. Then, I highlighted a band of affordable cities with housing centered on the $100 per square foot range, which would mean a 2,000 square foot house is about $200k.

As an added bonus, I added a column to calculate the change in house prices over the past year, just in case it helps us see if a city is on the way up or getting cheaper at the moment.

A chart like this is just a starting point – you’d need to read more about any place and then go visit in person before considering a move. But the idea is to start with data, and then do some fun research based on what you learn.

The Earth Awaits: Casting a Worldwide Net

House prices are a valuable metric, because they influence the cost of living more than almost anything else for the typical Mustachian. After all, biking and nature are always close to free, Costcos are available nationwide, and we probably care less than average about the costs of other services like valets and salons.

But there’s still plenty of value in looking at the bigger picture, considering more data points, and also being open to renting versus buying your housing. For this, I’m a big fan of a FIRE blogger-created site called The Earth Awaits, and we can take it for a test drive right now with the following search criteria:

Apartment type: Two bedroom (outside city center)

Temperature range: January lows not colder than 10F

The exact parameters don’t matter too much, as long as you don’t make them too narrow. The important thing is the resulting list, which is meant to give you ideas to research further. For example, that first simple search gave me this list:

Hey, that’s interesting. I like how the site shows the population right on the main list, because that provides a big clue to the “feel” of a city. I personally like the feel of a 50k-200k person town, so I might look into Fayetteville, Columbia or Athens. I’ve also been to Chattanooga and really like that place – who knew it was only about as expensive as Columbus Ohio?

In the end, your physical environment – the people, access to nature, urban features and the weather patterns – is probably the most important factor to get right in creating a happy life. The cost of living there is only one of the factors, and definitely not the most important one.

But if you choose carefully, you can probably slide yourself in the right direction along that “Nice for the Price” scale in order to get more from your life. Even if it just means making a move within your own city to live along a walking path, a little closer to work or to the people or places you care about most.

The key is just to remember that housing is like almost everything in life: It’s a choice that you get to make, and there are great rewards for putting some solid thought and effort into that choice.

Another Fun Example: Doing the Analysis on Tempe/Phoenix Arizona vs Denver

This is a fun exercise, because I’m currently living in the Phoenix area (more on that here)  that is way different than the Denver metro area where I normally live. We can start with the rough measure of housing cost per square foot across each region:

In other words, pretty close. Denver metro* is about 10% higher on average, but the variations from one neighborhood to another within any major city are much larger than that anyway.

So the other factors are more important. Both are surrounded by beautiful mountain recreation and get lots of sunshine, but the climates are famously quite different. Denver is more compact but Phoenix has nicer towns in the foothills around the outskirts.  In the end it’s just personal preference in weighting these various factors, and right now I kind of like the idea of both (Phoenix in winter but Colorado for the other three seasons)

More Adventurous: Let’s Try This in South America!

Going back to The Earth Awaits, if we repeat our earlier search but in South America, we get results like these:

Many of these spots have nice writeups if you click the “Details” button, and if anything sounds right for you, you can go on to learn much more.

It’s true that moving to a new country comes with all sorts of new learning experiences: citizenship and passports, laws and traditions and driver licenses, and of course having to cross an international border every time you want to return to your home country to visit family.

But guess what? If this stuff sounds daunting to you, it’s probably a sign that you need to do it more.

At its core, moving to a new place – even internationally – is just a series of relatively easy Adulting Puzzles. You type stuff into your computer, read the resulting stuff that pops up on your screen, and make the occasional phone call and visit to an official office. I had to do all the same stuff when moving from Canada to the US, alone and just six years out of high school myself.

Sure, it can feel like a “hassle” if you think of it the wrong way, but you know what’s a way, way bigger hassle? Living in a not-very-good place for life, or working an extra 15 years just to afford the higher cost of living in your current city, because you’re too scared to do a few weeks of work to make a big move to a better place.

If a rules-and-paperwork-hater like me can do it, almost anyone can.

While we covered a few examples of actual places in this article, the real purpose was to explain the thought process behind deciding when and where to move. And there are many of you out there besides me who can do the same thing, but better. And we’d love to hear from you!

If you have some favorite cities and countries for good living, or useful techniques for scoping them out, please share them in the comments. I strongly believe that the more we help each other find the right place and enjoy the planet more thoroughly and more efficiently, the better off we’ll all be. So let’s get moving.

* Denver metro on the Fed site includes all the suburbs rather than just the core city which is much smaller and more expensive, but the same is true for the nicer parts of Phoenix so I figure it’s a fair comparison)

He gives his own experience of geographic arbitrage as a good example of how he was able to move somewhere much less expensive than the big city to achieve his goals faster. Plenty of other FIRE types from the MMM age group did the same thing – they moved to Vermont, Bend, Bozeman etc. because those places were affordable and beautiful. The entire point of FIRE is to have the time to enjoy doing what you love and the most FIRE way to do this is by taking on hobbies in the great outdoors.

But here’s the thing: over the last ten years – and especially the last five – beautiful places with access to great low-cost outdoor recreation activities almost all fall into the data that the “US Home Price” graph hides.

Sure you can purchase a home in a climate-ravaged hell-scape or among the rows and rows of flat corn fields this country has to offer for a very reasonable price. Someplace that will make it extremely difficult to do all the many Mustachian things MMM has lauded through the years (biking, parks, outdoors, car-free life, etc.). Food deserts. Bankrupt suburbs or rural towns etc.

I don’t know that I’ve got better advice for these trying times however. I think if it were me, I would probably find a high-paying job in a city with reasonable rents and ease of a non-car lifestyle (funnily enough, in many cities, rents have actually grown at a fraction the rate of real estate). Seattle, Denver, Chicago, Portland, Philadelphia, DC are decent examples of this. NY, Boston, SF, LA, are not. Spend a decade or so (or however long it’ll take you) putting away as much money as you can and then reassess.

Maybe home prices will adjust way down everywhere? Maybe rent forever? Americans hate this idea, but the math makes more and more sense IMO in many parts of the country. Or maybe see if you can find a part of the country that will enable you to live a somewhat Mustachian life with low real estate costs. If it were me, I would be looking at the good parts of the Midwest – Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota. Places resilient to climate change with low housing costs and ample outdoor activities that maybe aren’t as high-brow as those of the wealthy class but still plenty enjoyable.

Sorry this was a bit of a rant, but while I think MMM is doing a lot to brush off the vast difference between the geographic arbitrage available to him and that available today, but I do still thing FIRE is possible for those of us in our 20s!

Mr. Money Mustache February 3, 2024, 5:40 pm

Good point about the bad policy – this seems to be the root cause of almost all the expensive housing in US cities. Whenever you have NIMBYs being allowed to complain to their city councils and get them to block the rezoning and building of new housing on land that THEY DO NOT OWN THEMSELVES, you end up with less new housing and potentially higher housing and rent prices due to the artificially restricted supply.

I prefer the option of almost no zoning, except for making sure the transportation network is designed for people rather than cars – since that is objectively proven to be healthier, happier and cheaper for everyone who ends up living there. It also allows you to fit far more housing.

So true about the way a city is zoned leading to housing shortages. I am watching a friends house while he is away. He has a 5 bed 3 bath house with 2 car garage that sits on roughly a 1/3 acre. It is just him and his cat when he is home. The house could easily fit 2 full families with the proper setup. However, getting the approval from the city would likely be impossible.

The larger issue with a redistribution of square footage or other zoning issues would be most people don’t want to buy a multi-family unit. The “American Dream” is not to own a rental unit (for the majority of people), and especially not to rent. Society looks down upon people who don’t own their own homes as failures. It takes a strong independent thinker to not cave to the group think.

The point about internet-generated movement is spot on and really significant. I’ve seen this firsthand in my hometown, which has changed dramatically in the past ten or fifteen years.

As recently as the early 2000s, my hometown was a sleepy seaside town off the beaten path, beautiful but known only by locals and a few others. This was before MapQuest, Google Maps, Zillow, online news, satellite car navigation, etc. If you didn’t already know what it was like there or have a personal connection to tell you, you’d never think to visit or buy property there.

There had always been a community of wealthy seasonal residents with vacation houses on the water, but the rest of the town was solidly middle class or even high blue collar. The local auto mechanics and construction workers lived in town and socialized with the white-collar locals.

But that all changed when the town was “discovered” and people from out of town began outbidding everyone else for the houses. The multigenerational continuity that made the community so strong has been broken by my millennial generation, since most of us couldn’t afford to buy the houses in town that our parents bought. It’s gotten so bad that the school is now at risk of closing for lack of kids, since no young families can afford to live there anymore.

I think that a similar phenomenon is happening at the global level. Housing costs are affected by the (lack of) supply, i.e. NIMBYism, but they’re also affected by demand generated by large-scale immigration. Other things being equal, an influx of new people makes housing more expensive. We see this in some parts of the US, but the effect is stronger in other places like Canada and Australia, where recent unprecedented amounts of immigration have coincided with huge increases in the cost of housing. The internet facilitates immigration by making it much easier for prospective immigrants to see what other places are like and what opportunities are available.

Another thing to watch out for is something we might call Irrational Local Driverphobia Syndrome (ILDS):

Being such an avid bikes-every-day-for-transportation person, I have ridden bikes in dozens or maybe even hundreds of cities around the world. And I’ve noticed two things:

– it has always worked out just fine. I got where I needed to go. – the residents of EVERY. SINGLE. CITY. have said the same thing: “Oh, it’s not safe to ride bikes HERE.. the drivers here are all crazy, and drinking and driving, and texting on their phone, and they hate cyclists.”

Yes, human-driven cars generally pretty dangerous. But you can mitigate most of that danger by choosing your route carefully, learning bicycle safety and getting lots of practice with bike control through trail and off-road-riding, and very importantly adding super bright flashing lights, front and rear, which you use at all times, sun, rain or shine.

In other words, although cars are the problem, most (although not all) bike crashes could have been avoided if the cyclist were skilled and vigilant enough to provide double the safety and caution – enough to cover both vehicles.

I think anecdotes are best discarded in favor of data. And I tried to do this once a while ago, although this article could use an updating with more recent statistics: https://www.mrmoneymustache.com/2012/06/07/safety-is-an-expensive-illusion/

The summary is that biking is SO GOOD for you, and not really all that dangerous in the big picture, that it has an effectively negative level of danger. i.e. your lifespan and healthspan increase when you do it.

But, if you’re in a rough urban area you gotta treat it like a hockey game where YOU are the puck and every moving thing is trying to hit you. So have the literal flashing lights installed on your bike in all directions, and have your figurative radar running on high as well, especially at every curb cut and intersection.

With proper awareness, you should be able to make it almost impossible for a car to hit you even if they are trying to do so (which of course they aren’t), because you’re riding so defensively.

It sounds harsh, but this is also the same thing it takes to be a good CAR driver and avoid accidents over a lifetime of driving.

She was driving down the street for work that was less than a mile and didn’t need to spend $800 a month on a car for 50k salary. All our investments went into low fee total market mutual funds. Our net worth is 6 times greater than when we started tracking in 2017.

For young readers, the earlier you start, the better and easier it will be to grow your investments. We were using high interest savings accounts which turned out to be a joke compared to investment options discussed here. I tried meme stocks and crypto coins but nothing worked as well as the consistent low fee funds and keeping our expenses low.

We’re not fire yet but we feel more comfortable and are able to handle increases in living expenses.
